بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

﴿الر تِلْكَ آياتُ الْكِتابِ وَقُرْآنٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (١)

[تقدم راجع ج ٨ ص ٣٠٤.] (Its meaning has already been given. See vol. 8, p. 304.) As for "الْكِتابِ" (al-Kitab, "the Book"), it has been said that it is a name for the genus of the earlier books, namely the Torah and the Gospel. Then He joined them with "الْكِتَابِ الْمُبِينِ" (al-Kitab al-Mubin, "the Clear Book"). It has also been said that "the Book" is the Qur'an, and that He combined two names for it.

"رُبَّ" لَا تَدْخُلُ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ

The particle "رُبَّ" (rubba, "many a" or "a few") does not come before a verb. If "مَا" (ma) is attached to it, this makes it suitable to come before a verb. You say: "رُبَمَا قَامَ زَيْدٌ" (rubbama qama Zayd, "Many a time Zayd stood up") and "وَرُبَمَا يَقُومُ زَيْدٌ" (wa-rubbama yaqumu Zayd, "and many a time Zayd stands up").

It is also permissible for "مَا" to be an indefinite noun meaning "شَيْء" (shay', "a thing"), with "يَوَدُّ" (yawaddu, "wishes") as its description. The meaning is: "رُبَّ شَيْءٍ يَوَدُّ الْكَافِرُ" (rubba shay'in yawaddu al-kafir, "many a thing the disbeliever wishes for").

Nafi' and 'Asim recited "رُبَمَا" with the "بّ" lightened (rubama, with a single "ba"). The rest recited it with the "بّ" doubled (rubbama). Both are dialects (lughatan). Abu Hatim said: the people of the Hijaz lighten "رُبَمَا", and a poet said:

*Rubbama darbatin bi-sayfin saqilin... bayna Busra wa-ta'natin najla'*

*Many a blow with a polished sword, between Busra and a wide spear-thrust.*

[[The verse is by 'Adi ibn al-Ra'laa' al-Ghassani. Busra is a town near Syria, the capital of Hawran, where a market was held in the pre-Islamic period. The author of Khizanat al-Adab said: "...The phrase 'bayna' (between) is idafa (construed) to Busra because Busra includes many places, meaning between the places of Busra and its surroundings. Al-Sharif al-Husayni related in his Hamasa: 'dun Busra' (below/before Busra). Here 'dun' means 'before' or 'behind'. Al-'Ayni said: it means 'near'." See Khizana, the 799th witness.]]

Tamim, Qays and Rabi'a pronounce it with the "بّ" doubled. It is also reported with various forms: "رَبَّمَا" and "رَبَمَا", and "رُبَتَمَا" and "رُبَّتَمَا", with the "بّ" both lightened and doubled. [[Ibn Hisham said in al-Mughni: "There are sixteen dialects of rubba: the 'ra' with damma (u) and with fatha (a), and each of these both doubled and lightened. The four forms with the feminine 'ta' (taa marbuta), either quiescent or vowelled, together with dropping it, make twelve. And the damma and fatha with the 'ya' quiescent, and both letters with damma, doubled and lightened."]]

Its original use is for few things, though it is sometimes used for many. That is, the disbelievers wish, at many times, that they had been Muslims. This is what the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa) said. From this is the poet's saying:

*Ala rubbama ahdat laka al-'aynu nazratan... qusaaruka minha annaha 'anka la tujdi*

*Behold, many a glance the eye has offered you; your final portion of it is that it does not avail you.*

[[That is, it does not suffice you. One says: "ma yajdi 'anka hadha", meaning "this does not avail you". In some copies of the original it reads "la tujza" with a zay, which also means "does not avail".]]

Some said: in this place it indicates few, because they said that in some situations and not in all of them, due to their preoccupation with punishment. And God knows best.

He said: "رُبَما يَوَدُّ" (rubama yawaddu, "many a time they wish"). It is only used for what has occurred, because of the certainty of the promise, as if it were a present reality that has already happened.

Abu al-Qasim al-Tabarani transmitted from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community will enter the Fire because of their sins, and they will remain in the Fire as long as God wills. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: 'We do not see that your affirming and your faith, which you opposed us in, has benefited you.' So no monotheist will remain but that God will bring him out of the Fire." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: "Many a time those who disbelieved will wish that they had been Muslims" (15:2).

Al-Hasan said: when the polytheists see the Muslims who have entered Paradise, and they did not see them in the Fire, they will wish that they had been Muslims.

Al-Dahhak said: this wishing is only at the moment of direct witnessing in the world, when guidance becomes clear to them from error.

It was also said: it is on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the honour of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers.

**Issue 1:** Concerning this verse there are two matters. The first is His saying, ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾, which is a threat to them.

(And hope distracts them), that is, it preoccupies them from obedience. It is said: "He distracted him from such-and-such," meaning he occupied him with it. And "he was distracted from the thing" (lahiya huwa 'an al-shay', yalha), meaning he was occupied with it.

(So they will come to know) when they see the Resurrection and taste the consequences of what they did. This verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by the sword.

**Issue 2:** In the Musnad of al-Bazzar, on the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four things are of wretchedness: hardness of the eye, hardness of the heart, long hope, and greed for this world." Long hope is a chronic disease and a persistent illness. When it takes hold of the heart, its temperament is corrupted and its treatment becomes severe. It never departs from the heart, and no remedy benefits it. Rather, it defeats the physicians, and the wise and the scholars despair of its cure.

The reality of hope is greed for this world, being absorbed in it, loving it, and turning away from the Hereafter.

It is also related (yurwā) from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The first of this Ummah was saved by certainty and asceticism, and its last will perish by stinginess and hope."

It is related from Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) that he stood on the steps of the Mosque of Damascus and said: "O people of Damascus, will you not listen to a sincerely advising brother of yours? Those before you used to gather much, build lofty buildings, and hope far. So their gathering became ruin, their buildings became graves, and their hope became delusion. Here is 'Ad, who filled the lands with people, wealth, horses and men. Who will buy their estate from me today for two dirhams?"

And he recited:

O you who hope for aims, though they are far from him,
and he supposes he will attain their farthest reach—

How will you succeed in what you hope for, woe to you,
when you are not even sure of attaining their nearest?

Al-Hasan said: "No servant prolongs hope except that he worsens his deeds." And he spoke the truth, may Allah be pleased with him! Hope makes one lazy in action, produces slackness and laxity, results in preoccupation and inertia, inclines one to the earth, and leans one toward desire. This is a matter witnessed by sight, so it needs no explanation, and its person need not be asked for proof. Just as shortness of hope incites action, urges haste, and spurs competition.

And We never destroyed a town but it had a decreed term known [to Us]. (4)

That is, a fixed appointed term, written for them in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

"Min" is an extra particle (ṣila), as in your saying: "Ma jā'anī min aḥadin" (no one came to me), meaning: they do not go beyond their term so as to exceed it, nor do they advance ahead of it. A parallel to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 201.]].

Said by the disbelievers of Quraysh to Muhammad (ﷺ) in a spirit of mockery; then they asked him to bring the angels as proof of his truthfulness. The word (lawma) here urges action, like (lawla) and (halla). Al-Farra' said: the mim in "lawma" is a substitute for the lam in "lawla." Similar to this are "istawla ʿala al-shay'" and "istawma ʿalayhi," and likewise "khalamtuhu" and "khallaltuhu," so that "khalamī" and "khalī" mean "my friend." On this basis, "lawma" may be used in the sense of a statement, as you say: "lawma Zayd ladaraba ʿAmr" (Were it not for Zayd, ʿAmr would have been struck). Al-Kisa'i said: "lawla" and "lawma" are the same in statement and in question. Ibn Muqbil said:

Were it not for shame and were it not for religion, I would have reproached you both
For some of what is in you both, since you both reproached my faults.

He means "lawla al-ḥayā'" (were it not for shame). Al-Nahhas related that "lawma," "lawla," and "halla" are one and the same. The lexicographers cited in support of this:

You count the hamstringing of the she-camel as the best of your glory,
O sons of Dawtara, rather than (were it not for) the armored warrior, the one wearing a helmet.

[[The verse is by Jarir, satirizing al-Farazdaq. "ʿAqr" means striking the legs of a she-camel with a sword. "Nayb" (with a kasra on the nun) is the plural of "nāb," meaning an aged she-camel. "Dawtara" is a bulky, base man who has no worth, a word of blame and insult. "Kamiyy" is a brave warrior who arms himself fully, because he covers himself with armor and helmet. "Muqannaʿ" is one who wears the helmet and visor.]]

That is, "halla ta'uddūna al-kamiyya al-muqannaʿa" (why do you not count the armored warrior, the one wearing a helmet?).

Qur'an Recitation of Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī: (مَا نُنَزِّلُ الْمَلائِكَةَ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ) ("We do not send down the angels except with truth"). Abū 'Ubayd (a grammarian and transmitter of readings) preferred this reading. Abū Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal read: "مَا تُنَزَّلُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ" ("the angels are not sent down"). The rest read: "مَا تَنَزَّلَ الْمَلَائِكَةُ" ("the angels do not descend"). Its underlying form is مَا تَتَنَزَّلُ with two tāʾs, one of which was elided for lightness. Al-Bazzī doubled the tāʾ (شدّد التاء). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, by analogy with the words: ﴿تَنَزَّلُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَالرُّوحُ﴾ ("The angels and the Spirit descend") [see vol. 20, p. 133].

The meaning of ﴿إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("except with truth") is: except with the Qur'an. It is also said: with the message, according to Mujāhid. Al-Ḥasan said: except with punishment, if they do not believe.

﴿وَمَا كَانُوا إِذًا مُنْظَرِينَ﴾ ("and they would not have been given respite then"): that is, if the angels descended to destroy them, they would not have been granted a reprieve, and their repentance would not have been accepted.

It is also said: the meaning is that if the angels descended to bear witness for you, and they disbelieved after that, they would not be given respite.

The origin of "إِذًا" is إِذْ أَنْ, meaning "in that case" (حِينَئِذٍ). Then أَنْ was attached to it, and because the hamza was felt to be heavy, they elided it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

(And indeed We are its guardians) from having anything added to it or taken away from it. Qatadah and Thabit al-Bunani said: God preserved it from the devils adding falsehood to it or removing truth from it. He, glorified be He, undertook its preservation, and so it has remained preserved. In another place He said: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 188.]], so He entrusted its preservation to them, and they altered and changed it.

Our shaykh, the jurist and imam Abu al-Qasim Abdullah, reported to us from his father, the shaykh, the jurist, the imam, the hadith scholar Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Khalaf ibn Ma'zuz al-Kumi al-Tilimsani, who said: It was read to the learned shaykha [[In MS ya: the righteous.]] Fakhr al-Nisa' Shuhda, daughter of Abu Nasr [[In MS waw: Abu Bakr.]] Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Dinawari, at her residence in Dar al-Salam, at the end of Jumada al-Akhira in the year five hundred and sixty-four. It was said to her: The most honoured shaykh, the active one, naqib al-nuqaba' Abu al-Fawaris Tarrad ibn Muhammad al-Zayni informed you by reading to him while you were listening, in the year four hundred and ninety, saying: Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Ibrahim informed us, Abu Ali Isa ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Umar ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Jurayj, known as al-Tumari, told us, al-Husayn ibn Fahm told us, who said: I heard Yahya ibn Aktham say: Al-Ma'mun, who was then a prince, held a session of inquiry, and into the crowd entered a Jewish man, well dressed, handsome of face, and pleasant of scent. He said: He spoke and expressed himself very well. He said: When the session dispersed, al-Ma'mun summoned him and said to him: "An Israelite?" He said: Yes. He said to him: "Embrace Islam, and I will do for you and provide for you," and he promised him. He said: "My religion is my fathers' religion!" and he departed. He said: When a year had passed, he came to us as a Muslim. He spoke on jurisprudence and spoke very well. When the session dispersed, al-Ma'mun summoned him and said: "Are you not our companion of yesterday?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What was the cause of your Islam?" He said: "I left your presence and wished to test these religions, and you see that I have good handwriting. So I went to the Torah and copied three copies of it, adding to them and removing from them, and I placed them in the synagogue, and they were bought from me. Then I went to the Gospel and copied three copies, adding to them and removing from them, and I placed them in the church, and they were bought from me. Then I went to the Qur'an and made three copies, adding to them and removing from them, and I placed them among the copyists (warraqin). They leafed through them, and when they found in them the addition and the omission, they threw them aside and did not buy them. So I knew that this is a preserved Book, and this was the cause of my Islam." Yahya ibn Aktham said: I performed the pilgrimage that year, met Sufyan ibn Uyayna, and related the report to him. He said to me: "Its confirmation is in the Book of God, mighty and majestic." I said: "In which passage?" He said: "In the saying of God, blessed and exalted, concerning the Torah and the Gospel: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of God﴾, so He made its preservation their responsibility and it was lost. And the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾, so God, the Mighty and Majestic, preserved it for us and it was not lost."

It was also said: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ means: guarding Muhammad ﷺ from fabricating against Us, or Us from his fabricating against Him. Or: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ means: from being plotted against or killed. Its parallel is: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 242.]].

The word "nahnu" (we) may be in the nominative position as the subject of the inchoative, with "nazzalna" (We sent down) as the predicate, and the whole clause as the predicate of "inna" (indeed). It is also permissible for "nahnu" to be a emphatic pronoun for the subject of "inna" in the accusative position, and it is not a separating pronoun (fasila), because what follows it is not a definite noun but a clause, and clauses serve as qualifiers for indefinite nouns, so their ruling is the ruling of indefinite nouns.

The meaning: "And We certainly sent (messengers) before you," with the object omitted. "Al-Shiya'" is the plural of "shi'ah," which means a community (ummah), i.e., among their nations; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: "among their sects." The shi'ah is a group or party of people who are bound together and united in their word. Thus al-Shiya' means factions, and from this is the verse ﴿or to confuse you into factions﴾ [1]. Its origin is derived from al-shiyaa' (kindling), which is small pieces of firewood with which larger logs are set alight, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am. Al-Kalbi said: the shiya' here means "villages" (al-qura).

[1] See vol. 7, p. 9.
This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: just as these polytheists have done to you, so too was done to those messengers who came before you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 12–13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus We cause it to enter﴾, i.e. misguidance, disbelief, mockery and polytheism. "Into the hearts of the criminals" from your people, related from al-Hasan, Qatadah and others. That is: just as We caused it to enter the hearts of those earlier sects of the ancients, so We cause it to enter the hearts of the polytheists of your people, so that they do not believe in you, just as those before them did not believe in their messengers. Ibn Jurayj related from Mujahid that he said: "We cause the denial (al-takdhib) to enter." And al-salk (sulk): the insertion of one thing into another, like inserting the thread into the needle's eye. It is said: salakahu yaslukuhu salkan and sulukan, and aslakahu islakan. And salaka al-tariq sulukan and salkan, and aslakahu (he entered it). The thing into another thing is similar, and the thing likewise, and the spear, and the thread into the pearl; all of these are fa'ala and af'ala. ʿAdi ibn Zayd said:

"And they have led you (salakuka) on a difficult day" [[This is the second half of the verse, as in al-Lisan and Shu'ara' al-Nasraniyya:

"And I was your opponent, I did not turn back."]]

And al-silk (with a kasra) is the thread. In the verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya and the Mu'tazila. It is also said: the meaning is "We cause the Qur'an to enter into their hearts, so they deny it." Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah said, and this is the view on which most of the exegetes agree, and it is the more binding argument against the Mu'tazila. And from al-Hasan also: "We cause the Reminder (al-dhikr) to enter, as a binding of the proof," mentioned by al-Ghaznawi.

(And the way of the ancients has already passed) i.e. the sunnah of Allah has passed concerning the destruction of the disbelievers, so how close these people are to destruction. It is also said: "the way of the ancients has passed" with the like of what these people did of denial and disbelief, so they follow those [earlier ones].

It is said: ẓalla yaf'alu kadhā (ظَلَّ يَفْعَلُ كَذَا), meaning he does it during the daytime. The verbal noun is al-ẓulūl (الظُّلُولُ), that is: if they were granted what they demanded of the signs, they would persist in disbelief and make excuses with imaginings, just as they said of the inimitable Qur'an that it is sorcery. "Ya'ruju" (يَعْرُجُونَ) comes from ʿaraja, ya'ruju, meaning he ascended. Al-maʿārij (الْمَعَارِجُ) are the ascending means, that is: if they ascended to the sky and witnessed the malakūt (the unseen dominion) and the angels, they would still persist in disbelief. This is related from al-Hasan and others.

It is also said that the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the polytheists, and the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" refers to the angels, who go and come. That is: if it were uncovered for these people until they witnessed doors in the sky through which the angels ascend and descend, they would say: "We have seen with our eyes what has no reality." This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada.

The meaning of "sukkirat" (سُكِّرَتْ) is: blocked by sorcery; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Al-Ḥasan said: "suḥirat" (سُحِرَتْ), that is, bewitched. Al-Kalbī said: our sights were covered; and from him also: they became blind. Qatada said: they were seized. Al-Mu'arrij said: "dīra bina," from al-dawarān (rotation), meaning our sights became drunken. Juwaybir said: they were deceived. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "sukkirat" means covered and veiled. From this is the saying of the poet:

"A sun rose over it, a helmet upon it,
and the eye of the heat-haze became drunk."

Mujāhid said: "sukkirat" means restrained. From this is the saying of Aws ibn Ḥajar:

"So I became one who stood on a sleepless night,
which is neither clear nor intoxicating."

[[In al-Lisān, under the root s-k-r: "jadhilat," with the letters jīm and dhāl both vowelled with fatḥa; the meaning of "jadhil" is to stand firm and remain unmoving. And a night ṭalq is one that is bright, with neither cold nor heat, neither rain nor chill.]]

I say: these sayings are close in meaning, and what unites them is your saying: "muni'at" (it was prevented). Ibn ʿUzayz said: "sukkirat abṣāruna" means our sights were blocked; it is from your saying, "sakartu al-nahr" when you block the river. It is also said that it is from the intoxication of drink, as if the eye is affected by what affects the drinker when he becomes intoxicated. Ibn Kathīr read "sakirat" with a light pronunciation, and the rest read it with the doubled letter.

It has also been said that the light form is from the intoxication of drink, and the doubled form means "they were seized." Al-Māwardī mentioned both.

It is also said: it is what appears to a person from weakness of sight when intoxicated by drink.]] Al-Farrāʾ said: whoever reads "sukirat" takes it from the sukūr of the wind [[its stillness after blowing]]. It is also said that the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the polytheists, and the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" refers to the angels, who go and come. That is: if it were uncovered for these people until they witnessed doors in the sky through which the angels ascend and descend, they would say: "We have seen with our eyes what has no reality." This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada.

Al-Kalbī said: our sights were covered; and from him also: they became blind. Qatada said: they were seized. Al-Mu'arrij said: "dīra bina," from al-dawarān (rotation), meaning our sights became drunken. Juwaybir said: they were deceived. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "sukkirat" means covered and veiled. From this is the saying of the poet:

"A sun rose over it, a helmet upon it,
and the eye of the heat-haze became drunk."

Mujāhid said: "sukkirat" means restrained. From this is the saying of Aws ibn Ḥajar:

"So I became one who stood on a sleepless night,
which is neither clear nor intoxicating."

[[In al-Lisān, under the root s-k-r: "jadhilat," with the letters jīm and dhāl both vowelled with fatḥa; the meaning of "jadhil" is to stand firm and remain unmoving. And a night ṭalq is one that is bright, with neither cold nor heat, neither rain nor chill.]]

When He mentioned the disbelief of the disbelievers and the powerlessness of their idols, He mentioned the perfection of His power, so that it would serve as evidence for His oneness.

The names of these constellations are: al-Hamal, al-Thawr, al-Jawza', al-Saratan, al-Asad, al-Sunbula, al-Mizan, al-Aqrab, al-Qaws, al-Jaddi, al-Dalw, and al-Hut. The Arabs regarded knowledge of the positions of the stars and their gates (anwa', the rising and setting of mansions) as among the most noble sciences, and they used them to find their way, to determine times, and to predict fertility and drought. They said: the celestial sphere has twelve constellations, and each constellation is two and a half mil (a measure of distance).

The root meaning of buruj is manifestation, and from it comes tabarruj (a woman's displaying of her adornment), by showing her finery. This meaning has already been discussed in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 284.]].

Others said: "buruj" means palaces and dwellings in which there are guards, which Allah created in the sky. And Allah knows best.

﴿And We have adorned it﴾, meaning the sky, as He said in Surat al-Mulk: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 210.]]. ﴿For the observers﴾, that is, for those who take heed and reflect.

﴿And We guarded them from every accursed devil.﴾ (17) Meaning: stoned (*marjum*). *Al-rajm* is pelting with stones. It was also said that *al-rajm* means cursing and expelling. When Allah the Exalted sent Jesus, He guarded three heavens from them until the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). After his mission, He guarded all of them, and they were shielded from the devils by shooting stars. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said the same. Ibn Abbas said: "The devils were not barred from the sky. They would enter it, steal news of it, and convey it to the soothsayers (*kahana*). They would add nine lies to every word, and they would tell it to the people of the earth. The one word was true and the nine were false. When people saw something of what they had said come true, they believed them in what they brought. When Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. إِلاَّ مَنِ اسْتَرَقَ السَّمْعَ فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهابٌ مُبِينٌ ﴿18﴾

﴿Except one who steals a hearing, and a clear flaming fire pursues him.﴾

That is, "But whoever steals a hearing, that is, a brief snatching," so this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it). It was also said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: except from among those [devils] who steal a hearing. That is, We guarded the sky from the devils so that they could not hear anything of the revelation or of other things, except one who steals a hearing, for We did not guard it against him from hearing news of the heavens other than revelation. As for revelation, he hears nothing of it, because of His saying: "Indeed, they are removed from hearing" [see vol. 13, p.]. When the devils hear something that is not revelation, they throw it to the soothsayers (kahanah, soothsayers claiming knowledge of the unseen) in less than the blink of an eye. Then the shooting stars follow them and either kill them or cause them to be afflicted (takhbil, impairing their faculties or limbs; al-khabl, with the yaa' sukun, means corruption of the limbs). This was related by al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-atba'ahu shihabun mubin﴾ (then a clear flaming fire pursued him). Atba'ahu means he overtook him and caught up with him. Shihab means a luminous star. Likewise, "shihab thaqib" (a piercing flame). His saying, "with a flaming brand (shihab qabas)" [see vol. 13, p. 156], means with a blaze of fire at the top of a stick, as said by Ibn 'Uzayr. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in pursuit of a demon (ifritah),
marked (musawwam) in the darkness of the night, darting down (munqadib)."

The star was called shihab because of its brightness, resembling fire. It was also said: shihab is a flame of fire, a brand (qabas) for the people of the earth, which burns them; and when it burns, it does not return, just as fire, when it burns, does not return. Unlike a star, which, when it burns, returns to its place. Ibn 'Abbas said: The devils ascend in groups seeking to steal a hearing, and the rebellious one among them (al-marid) separates himself and rises higher, and then a shihab is hurled at him and strikes his forehead or his nose or whatever God wills, and he catches fire. He then comes to his companions while he is burning, and says: "It was such-and-such from the revelation." So those (companions) go to their brethren among the soothsayers and add nine more to it, and they tell the people of the earth about it: "The word is true, and the nine are false." When they see something of what they had said come to pass, they believe them in everything they brought of their lies. This meaning will come up as a report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Surah Saba' [see vol. 14, p. 295], God willing, Exalted is He.

There is disagreement over whether the shihab kills or not. Ibn 'Abbas said: the shihab wounds, burns, and impairs, but does not kill. Al-Hasan and a group said: it kills. According to this view, regarding their being killed by the shihab before the devils cast the hearing they stole to the jinn, there are two opinions. One: they are killed before they pass on to others what they have stolen by hearing; according to this, the news of the heavens does not reach anyone other than the prophets, and for this reason soothsaying has ceased. The second: they are killed after they pass on to other jinn what they have stolen by hearing; and for this reason they return to stealing it, and if it had not reached them, stealing would have ceased and burning would have ceased. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. I say: the first opinion is more sound, as will be explained in Surah al-Saffat.

There is disagreement over whether the hurling of shihab occurred before the Mission (al-mab'ath, the prophetic commission). Most scholars said yes. It was also said: no, rather that happened only after the Mission. The explanation of this issue will come in Surah al-Jinn [see note (1)], God willing, Exalted is He, and also in al-Saffat.

Al-Zajjaj said: The hurling with shihab is among the signs of the Prophet (ﷺ) that occurred after his birth, because the poets of old did not mention it in their poetry, and they did not liken a swift thing to it as they likened things to lightning and to torrents. It is not far-fetched to say: the falling of stars existed in ancient times, but it was not a hurling for the devils; then it became a hurling when the Prophet (ﷺ) was born. The scholars said: we see the falling of stars, and it is possible that it is as we see it, and then it becomes fire when it reaches a devil. And it is possible to say: they are pelted with a flame of fire from the air, so it appears to us as a star that moves.

In the language, shihab means a blazing fire.

Abu Dawud related from 'Amir al-Sha'bi, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, the devils were pelted with stars with which they had never been pelted before. They came to 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi and said: "The people have become terrified, and they have freed their slaves and let their livestock loose because of what they saw among the stars." He said to them, and he was a blind man: "Do not hurry; look. If the stars are those that are known, then they are a sign of the end of people, and if they are not known, then they are from a new event." They looked, and behold, they were stars not known, so they said: "This is from a new event." They did not wait until they heard of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾. This is also among His favours, and among what indicates the perfection of His power. Ibn 'Abbas said: We spread it out over the surface of the water, as He said: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 10, and p. 201.]], meaning He spread it. And He said: ﴿And We spread the earth out, and how excellent are the ones who spread it out﴾ [[See vol. 71, p. 52.]]. This refutes whoever claims that it is like a sphere. This has already been discussed [[See vol. 9, p. 280.]].

(﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾) mountains that are fixed, so that it does not shake with its inhabitants.

(﴿And We caused to grow in it of every thing a measured amount﴾) meaning, determined and known. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. He said "mawzun" (measured) because weight is the means by which the quantity of a thing is known. The poet said:

Before meeting you I was a man of strength; with me, every adversary has his scale.

Qatadah said: mawzun means divided out. Mujahid said: mawzun means counted. It is said: "This is a measured speech," meaning versified, not scattered. On this view, the meaning is that We caused to grow in the earth what is weighed of gems, animals and minerals. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said regarding animals: ﴿And He caused them to grow a goodly growth﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 69.]]. The purpose of causing to grow is bringing into being and creating. It has also been said: "We caused to grow in it" meaning in the mountains "of every thing measured": of gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, and even arsenic and kohl; all of these are weighed by weight. This meaning was narrated from al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. It has also been said: We caused the fruits to grow in the earth, of what is measured by volume and weighed. And it has been said: what is weighed for the exchange of prices, because it is greater in value and more widely beneficial than what has no price.

(﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood﴾) meaning the foods and drinks by which they live; its singular is ma'ishah (with a sukun on the ya'). From it is the saying of Jarir:

"You burden me with the livelihood of the family of Zayd, and who will provide me with the thin bread and the mustard?"

[[The ruqaq are wide thin loaves; the sinab is mustard mixed with raisins, eaten as a relish.]]

The original form is ma'ishah on the pattern of maf'alah (with the ya' vowelled). This was discussed earlier in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 167.]]. It has also been said that it means clothing; this was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that it means the management of the means of sustenance during the span of life. Al-Mawardi said: and this is the apparent meaning.

(﴿And [We made for you] those whom you do not provide sustenance for﴾) meaning the beasts and livestock; this was said by Mujahid. Also according to him, they are the slaves and children, concerning whom Allah said: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 252.]]. The word "man" (those) may include slaves and beasts when they are combined, because when those who reason and those who do not reason are combined, those who reason take precedence. That is, We made for you therein livelihoods, slaves, female slaves, beasts and children whom We provide for and whom you do not provide for. On this interpretation, "man" is in the accusative position, as Mujahid and others said. It has also been said that it refers to wild animals. Sa'id said: Mansur recited to us "wa man lastum lahu biraziqin" and said: the wild animals. On this view, "man" is used for what does not reason, as in ﴿Of them is one that walks on its belly﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 291.]] and so on. It is in the genitive position, in coordination with the kaf and mim in His saying "lakum" (for you). This is considered an unsound construction according to the Basran grammarians, since they do not permit coordinating a noun with an attached pronoun without repeating the preposition, as in "marartu bihi wa-bi-Zayd" (I passed by him and by Zayd). "Marartu bihi wa-Zayd" is not permitted except in poetry, as the poet said:

"Today you have approached us, deriding us and insulting us; so go away, for what is wrong with you and with the days is strange."

This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 300.]] and in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 3 and following.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 21:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures﴾. That is: and there is not any thing of the provisions of creatures and their benefits except that with Us are its treasures. He means the rain sent down from the sky, for by it is the growth of everything. Al-Hasan said: "The rain is the treasures of everything." It has also been said: "The khaza'in (treasures) are the keys (al-maqatih)," meaning that in the sky are the keys of the provisions. This was said by al-Kalbi. The meaning is one.

﴿And We send it down only in a known measure﴾. That is: but We do not send it down except according to Our will and according to the need of creatures for it, as He said: "And if Allah had expanded the provision for His servants, they would have committed excess in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills" [[See vol. 16, p. 27.]]. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hakam ibn Utaybah and others that there is no year with more rain than another, but Allah distributes it as He wills: a people are given rain while others are deprived, and perhaps the rain falls in the seas and the deserts. The khaza'in (treasures) is the plural of khizana (storehouse), which is the place where a person keeps his wealth. Khizana is also the verbal noun of kharana, yakhzunu. Whatever is in a person's storehouse is set aside for him; likewise, what the Lord is able to bestow is as if it is set aside with Him. This was said by al-Qushayri. Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, from his grandfather, that he said: "In the Throne there is a likeness of everything Allah created on land and sea." And this is the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures﴾.

The inzal (sending down) here means initiation and bringing into existence, as in His saying: "And He sent down for you eight pairs of cattle" [[See vol. 15, p. 234.]] and His saying: "And We sent down iron, wherein is great might" [[See vol. 17, p. 260.]]. It has also been said: inzal means giving, and He called it sending down because the rulings of Allah only descend from the sky.

There are five issues concerning this.

The first concerns God's words, ﴿And We sent the winds﴾. The common reading is "al-riyah" in the plural. Hamzah read it in the singular, because the meaning of "rih" (wind) is also plural, even though its form is singular. It is said: "The wind came from every direction." It is also said: "Arḍ sabasib" [[al-sabasib: a flat, far-reaching land.]] and "thawb akhlaq," and the Arabs do this with anything that is broad. As for the reasoning behind the common reading, God described the winds as ﴿fertilizing﴾ (lawaqih), which is plural. The meaning of lawaqih is "pregnant" (hawamil), because the winds carry water, earth, clouds, goodness and benefit. Al-Azhari said: "God made the wind a lāqiḥ (fertilizing) because it carries the clouds, that is, it lifts them and directs them, then it stirs them [[marrat al-rih al-sahab: when the wind has released rain from it.]] so that they release their rain. God said: ﴿until, when they have carried heavy clouds﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 228.]], meaning they carried them. A she-camel is laqiḥ, and camels are lawaqih, when they have carried fetuses in their wombs." It was also said that lawaqih means mulaqqiḥah (causing fertilization), which is the original sense, but they only fertilize while they are themselves fertilized, as if the winds were impregnated with goodness. It was said: dhawat luqḥ (possessors of pollen). All of these are valid: some of them fertilize trees, as in the expressions "ʿīshah rāḍiyah" (a pleasing life), meaning one in which there is contentment, and "layl nā'im" (a sleeping night), meaning one in which there is sleep. Others bring the clouds. It is said: "The she-camel became pregnant (laqiḥat, with kasra) luqḥan and luqāḥan (with fatḥa), so she is lāqiḥ. The stallion impregnated her (alqaḥahā al-faḥl), meaning he delivered water to her and she conceived it." So the winds are like the stallion to the clouds. Al-Jawhari said: "Riyāḥ lawāqiḥ," and one does not say "malāqiḥ," which is one of the rare forms. Al-Mahdawi related from Abu ʿUbaydah that lawāqiḥ means malāqiḥ, holding that it is the plural of mulqiḥah and mulqiḥ, with its extra letters dropped. It was said that it is the plural of lāqiḥah and lāqiḥ, in the sense of "possessing fertilization" by way of attribution. It is also possible that the meaning of lāqiḥ is "pregnant." The Arabs say of the south wind that it is lāqiḥ and pregnant, and of the north wind that it is pregnant and barren. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: God sends the bearer of good tidings (al-mubashshirah), and it sweeps the earth clean (taqumm al-arḍ qamman). Then He sends the stirring wind (al-muthīrah), which stirs up the clouds. Then He sends the gathering wind (al-mu'allifah), which gathers them. Then He sends the fertilizing winds (al-lawāqiḥ), which fertilize the trees. It was also said: the fertilizing winds (al-malāqiḥ) are those that carry the dew and then spill it into the clouds, and when it gathers in them it becomes rain. From Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The south wind is from Paradise, and it is the fertilizing wind that God mentioned in His Book, and in it are benefits for people." It is also related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Whenever the south wind blows, God causes a copious spring to gush forth by means of it." Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash said: "Not a drop falls from the cloud until the four winds have acted upon it: the eastern wind (al-ṣabā) stirs it, the western wind (al-dabūr) fertilizes it, the southern wind (al-janūb) brings it forth, and the northern wind (al-shamāl) disperses it."

The second issue: Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam related from Malik, and the wording is that of Ashhab, that Malik said: God said: "And We sent the winds fertilizing," so in my view the fertilization of wheat is that it forms its grain-heads and ears (yuḥabbib wa-yusanbil). I do not know what happens to it when it dries in its sheaths, but it forms grain so that if it dries at that point it is not corrupt, but has no good in it. The fertilization of all trees is that they bear fruit, then some of it falls and some of it remains. This is not by means of "tawrīd" (budding). Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Malik relied in this interpretation on comparing the fertilization of trees with the fertilization of pregnancy, since when the child is conceived, shaped, and given the spirit, it is in the same position as the forming of fruit and its ears, because it is called by a name shared by every pregnancy, which is liqāḥ (fertilization). On this the hadith came: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the sale of grain until it hardens." Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: among the scholars, "ibār" (pollination) for palm trees means tilqīḥ (pollination), which is taking some of the male pollen of the palm and placing it among the female flower clusters.

The meaning of this for the rest of the fruits is the emergence of the fruit from the fig and other trees, until the fruit is visible and can be seen. The criterion for Malik and his companions with regard to fruit that is designated as male is the designation, and for what is not designated, that what is meant to remain of its flowering remains and what is meant to fall falls. The criterion for crops is their emergence from the ground, as Malik said. It is related from him that their pollination is their forming grains. The scholars have not disagreed that when the female flowers of an orchard have split open, but its pollination is delayed while others of similar condition have been pollinated, its ruling is the ruling of what has been pollinated, because its time for pollination has come and its fruit is visible after being hidden inside the sheath. If part of the orchard is pollinated, what has not been pollinated follows it, just as when an orchard's produce has become good, the rest of the orchard follows that goodness in the permissibility of its sale.

The third issue: all the imams related from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Whoever buys a palm tree after it has been pollinated, its fruit belongs to the one who sold it, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise. Whoever buys a slave, his property belongs to the one who sold him, unless the buyer stipulates it." Our scholars said: the fruit that has been pollinated does not enter the sale along with the roots except by stipulation, because it is a present, existing thing that is enclosed, and it is generally safe from falling. This is unlike that which has not been pollinated, since its falling is not secure, so its existence is not established, and so it is not permissible for the seller to stipulate it or to except it, because it is like the fetus. This is the well-known position of the school of Malik. It was said: it is permissible to except it, which is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

The fourth issue: if the palm trees are sold and the fruit remains with the seller, it is permissible for the buyer of the trunk to buy the fruit before it is ripe, according to the well-known view of Malik, and it is considered to have the status of a subordinate, even if it is subject to a separate contract. Another report from him says it is not permissible. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi, Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, the Zahiris, and the jurists of hadith. It is also the more apparent reading of the hadiths prohibiting the sale of fruit before it has become good.

The fifth issue: among what relates to this topic is the prohibition on selling the malāqiḥ. The malāqiḥ are stallion camels, singular mulqiḥ. The malāqiḥ are also the female camels that have young in their wombs, singular mulqaḥah (with fatḥa on the qāf). The malāqīḥ are what is in the wombs of she-camels of fetuses, singular malqūḥah, from the saying "luqiḥat," like "al-maḥmūm" from "ḥumma" (one with fever) and "al-majnūn" from "junna" (one who is mad). It is in this matter that the prohibition came. There is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he forbade al-majr, which is the sale of what is in the wombs of females. He forbade al-maḍāmīn and al-malāqīḥ. Abu ʿUbayd said: al-maḍāmīn are what is in the wombs, which are the fetuses, and al-malāqīḥ are what is in the loins of stallions. This is the view of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and others. It was also said the reverse: that al-maḍāmīn are what is on the backs of camels, and al-malāqīḥ are what is in the wombs of females. This is the view of Ibn Ḥabib and others. Whichever of the two meanings is correct, the scholars of the Muslims agree that it is not permissible.

Al-Muzani related from Ibn Hisham, as evidence that al-malāqīḥ are what is in the wombs, a verse by one of the Bedouins:

"My longings are fetuses in the bellies, they produce what was fertilized after some time."

Al-Jawhari cited on this a verse of the rajaz meter by a reciter:

"Indeed we found the driving of the scattered camels better than the groaning and the she-camels of the wanderers,
and the number of the year and the coming year, fertilized in the belly of a pregnant old she-camel."

God's words, ﴿So We sent down from the sky﴾, meaning from the clouds. Everything that is above you and shades you is called "samāʾ" (sky). It is also said: from the direction of the sky.

﴿water﴾, meaning rain.

﴿and We gave it to you to drink﴾, meaning We made that rain for your watering, for the drinking of your livestock, and for your land. It is also said that saqā and asqā have the same meaning. It is also said that they differ, and this has been discussed previously [[See vol. 1, p. 417.]].

﴿and you are not its keepers﴾, meaning its treasuries are not with you. We are the keepers of this water: We send it down when We wish and withhold it when We wish. Similar to this are God's words: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 39 onward.]], and ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, then We made it settle in the earth, and indeed We are able to remove it﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 109.]]. Sufyan said: "You are not preventers of rain."

Namely, the earth and whoever is upon it, and nothing remains besides Us. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned﴾. So the ownership of everything belongs to Allah the Exalted. But He has granted His servants possessions, and when they die, their claims come to an end, so Allah is the Inheritor in this respect. It was also said: the "giving of life" in this verse refers to the bringing to life of the drop of semen in the wombs. As for the resurrection, He mentioned it after this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the One who will gather them﴾.

**Issue 1:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly know those of you who go before, and We certainly know those who come later﴾. On this there are eight interpretations.

First: "those who go before" are the created beings up to the present day, and "those who come later" are those not yet created. This is said by Qatadah, Ikrimah, and others.

Second: "those who go before" are the dead, and "those who come later" are the living. This is said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak.

Third: "those who go before" are those from earlier generations of the Muhammad's community, and "those who come later" are the community of Muhammad ﷺ. This is said by Mujahid.

Fourth: "those who go before" are those who advance in obedience and goodness, and "those who come later" are those who lag in disobedience and evil. This is also said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Fifth: "those who go before" are those who stand in the front ranks of battle, and "those who come later" are those who hang back from them. This is said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

Sixth: "those who go before" are those who were killed in jihad, and "those who come later" are those who were not killed. This is said by al-Qurazi.

Seventh: "those who go before" are the first of creation, and "those who come later" are the last of creation. This is said by al-Sha'bi.

Eighth: "those who go before" are those who stand in the front rows of prayer, and "those who come later" are those who hang back in it because of women.

All of this is known to God, Exalted is He, for He knows everything that exists and everything that does not, and He knows whom He will create and what He will create until the Day of Resurrection. However, the eighth opinion is the occasion of revelation of the verse, based on what al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu al-Jawza', from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There was a woman, beautiful and among the most beautiful of people, who prayed behind the Messenger of God ﷺ. Some of the people would move forward so that they would be in the first row, so as not to see her, and some of them would hang back so that they would be in the last row. When he bowed, he would look at her from under his armpit. So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And We certainly know those of you who go before, and We certainly know those who come later﴾."

It is also narrated from Abu al-Jawza' without mention of Ibn Abbas. And this is more sound [In variant manuscript: "al-Sahih" (the sound)].

**Issue 2:** This verse indicates the virtue of the beginning of the prescribed time (awwal al-waqt) for prayer, and the virtue of the first row (al-saff al-awwal). The Prophet ﷺ said: "If people knew what there is in the call (to prayer) and the first row, and they could find no way to obtain them except by drawing lots, they would draw lots for them." When a man comes at the time of zawal (the sun's decline after its zenith) and sits down in the first row adjacent to the imam, he obtains three levels of merit: the beginning of the time, the first row, and proximity to the imam. If he comes at the time of zawal and sits down in the last row, or in any row behind the first, he has obtained the merit of the beginning of the time, but has missed the merit of the first row and of proximity. If he comes at the time of zawal and sits down in the first row but not the one next to the imam, he has obtained the merit of the beginning of the time and the merit of the first row, but has missed proximity to the imam. If he comes after zawal and sits down in the first row, he has missed the merit of the beginning of the time, but has obtained the merit of the first row and proximity to the imam. And so on.

Proximity to the imam is not for everyone. Rather, it is as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let those of you who have maturity and understanding stand closest to me," and the hadith continues. The place next to the imam should belong to the one who has this description. If someone else stands there, he should be moved back, and the one who deserves it should move forward to that place, because it is his right by the command of the Lawgiver, just as the mihrab is the place of the imam, whether one moves forward or back. This is what Ibn al-Arabi said.

I say: It is upon this that the saying of Umar, may God be pleased with him, is to be understood: "Move back, so-and-so! Move forward, so-and-so!" and then he would step forward and say the takbir.

It has also been narrated from Ka'b that a man of this community would prostrate and be forgiven, along with whoever is behind him. Ka'b would seek out the last row of the mosque, hoping for this, and he would mention that he had found it so in the Torah. This was recorded by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul.

More explanation of this subject will come, God willing, in Surat al-Saffat [See vol. 15, p. 137 onward.].

**Issue 3:** Just as this verse indicates the virtue of the first row in prayer, it likewise indicates the virtue of the first row in fighting. Standing against the enemy's throat, and a servant selling himself to God, Exalted is He, has no equal in deed. So advancing toward it is more excellent, and there is no disagreement about it, nor is it hidden.

No one would go ahead of the Messenger of God ﷺ into battle, because he was the bravest of people. Al-Bara' said: "By God, when the fighting grew fierce, we would take cover behind him, and the bravest of us was the one who stood level with him," meaning the Prophet ﷺ.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them﴾, meaning: for the reckoning and the recompense.

(﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾) has already been discussed. [[See vol. 1, pp. 287 and 279.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did certainly create man﴾, meaning Adam (peace be upon him), ﴿from clay of sounding (ṣalṣāl)﴾, i.e., from dry clay, related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Ṣalṣāl is clay of good quality (al-ṭīn al-ḥurr) mixed with sand, so that it rings (yataṣalṣal) when it dries; when it is baked by fire it becomes fakhkhār (pottery), related from Abu ʿUbayda. This is the saying of most of the exegetes. The philologists recited (the line of poetry):

"Like the running of the jingling wanderer" [[This is the second half of the verse. Its complete form, as in Lisan al-ʿArab:

ʿAnterīs taʿdū idhā massahā al-ṣawt... kaʿadw al-musalsil al-jawwāl]]

Mujahid said: it is foul-smelling clay, and al-Kisa'i preferred this. He said: it comes from the Arabic saying, ṣalla al-laḥm and aṣalla when it became foul-smelling, whether cooked or raw, yaṣillu ṣulūlan. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa said:

"That is a youth who gives away his pot; the rotten meat does not spoil in his presence."

And there is ṭīn ṣallāl and miṣlāl, meaning that it makes a sound when you strike it, as iron makes a sound. It was first dust, that is, with scattered parts; then it was moistened and became clay; then it was left until it became foul-smelling and became ḥama' masnūn, that is, changed; then it dried and became ṣalṣāl, according to the majority view. The explanation of this has already passed in al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, pp. 287 and 279.]]. Ḥama' is black clay; likewise ḥamʾa (with a sukūn). One says from it: ḥamaytu al-bi'r ḥamʾan (with sukūn) when you removed its silt. And ḥamiyat al-bi'r ḥamaʾan (with fatḥa) when its silt increased. And aḥmaʾtuhā iḥmāʾan: I threw out the silt, related from Ibn al-Sikkit. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-ḥamʾa (with sukūn of the mim) is like al-kamʾa (truffle). Its plural is ḥamaʾ, like tamra and tamr. And al-ḥama' is a verbal noun, like al-halaʿ and al-jazaʿ, and then it was named by it. And al-masnūn means changed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is moistened, foul-smelling dust, which was made into ṣalṣāl like pottery. Mujahid and Qatada had the same saying; they said: al-muntin means changed, from their saying: qad asanna al-māʾ when water changed, and from it [the Qur'an]: "yatasannah" [[See vol. 3, p. 288.]] and "māʾin ghayri āsin" [[See vol. 16, p. 236.]]. From it is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"My voice has given me saliva, not of a changed kind, like musk mixed into the water of grapes."

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is the changed, and its origin is from their saying: sanantu al-ḥajar ʿalā al-ḥajar when I rubbed one stone against another. What comes out of the two stones is called al-sanāna and al-sanīn, and from it al-misann. The poet said:

"Then I took her by the waist to the green dome, she walks, walking on polished marble, masnūn."

That is, rubbed and smoothed. It is related that Yazid ibn Muʿawiya said to his father: "Do you not see ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān courting your daughter?" Muʿawiya said: "And what did he say?" He said: he said:

"She is a flower like a pearl of the diver, separated from a hidden jewel."

Muʿawiya said: "He spoke the truth!" Yazid said: "He says:

'And when you trace her lineage, you will not find her
in a seat of noble qualities, lacking.'"

He said: "He spoke the truth!" Then he said: "Where is his saying: 'Then I took her by the waist...' the line?" Muʿawiya said: "He lied."

Abu ʿUbayda said: al-masnūn means poured, and it comes from the Arab saying: sanantu al-māʾ and other things over the face when I poured it. And al-sann is pouring. Ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: al-masnūn is moist, and this has the meaning of poured, because nothing is poured unless it is moist. Al-Naḥḥas said: this is a good saying, because one says: sanantu al-shayʾ, meaning I poured it. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ said: from it is the report related from ʿUmar that he used to pour the water over his face and not disperse it. Al-shann (with shīn) is scattering water, and with the unpointed sīn it is pouring it without scattering. Sibawayh said: al-masnūn is the shaped, taken from the sunna of the face, which is its form. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"She shows you the form of a face, separated, smooth, with no mole nor scar."

Al-sunna: the form. Al-muqarrafa: one close to the mixed-born. Al-nadab: the mark of wounds and scratches. His saying "not qarrana" means not mixed-born, chaste and noble. Khāl: a beauty spot; nadab: a mark of a wound.

Al-Akhfash said: al-masnūn is the raised and standing, from their saying: a masnūn face when it has length. It has been said that ṣalṣāl is for finely ground dust, related by al-Mahdawi. As for the one who says that ṣalṣāl is the foul-smelling, its origin is ṣalāl, and one of the two lāms was replaced by ṣād. And ﴿min ḥamaʾ﴾ explains the kind of ṣalṣāl, like your saying: I took this from a man of the Arabs.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾. That is, before Adam. Al-Hasan said: it means Iblis, whom God Most High created before Adam, peace be upon him. He was called "jinn" because he is hidden (tawarri) from the eyes. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Thabit, from Anas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God Most High fashioned Adam, peace be upon him, in Paradise, He left him for as long as God willed to leave him. Iblis began to circle around him and look at what he was. When he saw him hollow [ajwaf], he knew that he was a creature who could not control himself [[That is, who does not possess himself and restrain himself from desires. It was also said: who cannot repel whisperings from himself.]]."

(From the fire of the scorching wind [al-samum].) Ibn Mas'ud said: "The fire of the samum, from which God created the jinn, is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Hell." Ibn 'Abbas said: al-samum is the scorching wind that kills. And from him: it is a fire without smoke; thunderbolts (al-sawa'iq) come from it, and it is a fire that exists between the sky and the veil. When God decrees a matter, the thunderbolt tears through the veil and falls to where it was commanded. So the crash (al-hadda) [[al-hadda: the sound of a wall or the like falling; al-hadda: the sound of what falls from a cloud.]] that you hear is the rending of that veil. Al-Hasan said: the fire of the samum is a fire behind which there is a veil, and what you hear of the rumbling of the clouds is its sound. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: Iblis was from a tribe of the angels called the jinn, created from the fire of the samum among the angels. And the jinn mentioned in the Qur'an were created from a smokeless fire (marij min nar). I say: this requires examination, for it needs a chain of transmission that cuts off excuse, since such a matter is not said on the basis of opinion. Muslim has transmitted, from the hadith of 'Urwah, from 'A'isha, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless fire (marij min nar), and Adam was created from what has been described to you." So his saying "The angels were created from light" implies generality. And God knows best. Al-Jawhari said: marij min nar is a fire without smoke, from which the jinn were created; and al-samum is the scorching wind, which is feminine. It is said of it: "Our day was scorched (summa), so it is a scorched day (yawm masmum)," and the plural is sama'im. Abu 'Ubayda said: the samum is by day and may also be by night, while the harur is by night and may also be by day. Al-Qushayri said: the scorching wind was called samum because it enters the pores (masam) of the body with its subtlety.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verses 28–29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay, from black mud altered in form."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, then fall down to him in prostration.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 261, and p. 291 onward.]].

(Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay) i.e., from earth.

(So when I have proportioned him) i.e., when I have proportioned his creation and his form.

(And breathed into him of My [created] spirit) The nafkh (breathing) is the causing of wind to pass into a thing. The ruh (spirit) is a subtle body, and God has established the custom that life is created in the body together with that subtle body. Its reality is the attribution of a creation to the Creator: the ruh is a creation from among His creation, which He attributed to Himself as an honour and dignity, like His saying: "My earth, My heaven, My house, the she-camel of God, the month of God." Similar to this is ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾, which has already been explained in al-Nisa' [[See vol. 6, p. 22]]. In the book al-Tadhkirah we have mentioned the hadiths that indicate that the ruh is a subtle body, and that the nafs (soul) and the ruh are two names for one referent. This will come, God willing. As for one who says the ruh is life, he means: when life is placed into it.

(Then fall down to him in prostration) i.e., fall down before him, prostrating. This is a prostration of greeting and honour, not a prostration of worship. God may favour whom He wills, and He favoured the prophets over the angels. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 261, and p. 291 onward.]]. Al-Qaffal said: they were more excellent than Adam, and God tested them by ordering them to prostrate to him, as an exposure to great reward. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah. It was also said: they were commanded to prostrate to God at Adam's place, and Adam was a qiblah for them.

God may favour whom He wills, and He favoured the prophets over the angels. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 261, and p. 291 onward.]]. Al-Qaffal said: they were more excellent than Adam, and God tested them by ordering them to prostrate to him, as an exposure to great reward. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah. It was also said: they were commanded to prostrate to God at Adam's place, and Adam was a qiblah for them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 30–31:

His saying, exalted is He (﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together, / Except Iblis﴾), contains two issues.

The first: There is no doubt that Iblis was commanded to prostrate, according to His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 169]. What prevented him from that was arrogance and self-magnification, as its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 294]. Then it has been said: he was one of the angels, so the exception is from the genus (istithna' muttasil). And a people said: he was not one of the angels, so the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). All of this has been fully discussed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 294].

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Jann is the father of the jinn, and they are not shayatin (devils). The shayatin are the offspring of Iblis; they do not die except together with Iblis. The jinn do die, and among them are the believer and the disbeliever. So Adam is the father of mankind, al-Jann is the father of the jinn, and Iblis is the father of the shayatin. This was related by al-Mawardi. What has preceded in al-Baqarah is contrary to this, so reflect upon it there.

The second issue: The exception from a genus of a different genus is valid according to al-Shafi'i, so that if someone says, "I owe so-and-so a dinar except a garment," or "ten garments except a qafiz of wheat," and what is similar to that, it is accepted, and the value of the garment and the wheat does not drop from the sum due. The measured items (makilat), the weighed items (mawzunat) and the estimated items (muqaddarat) are equal in this. Malik and Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the exception of a measured item from a weighed item, and of a weighed item from a measured item, is permissible, so that if he excepts dirhams from wheat, or wheat from dirhams, it is accepted. But if he excepts valued items (muqawwamat) from measured or weighed items, or measured items from valued items, such as saying, "I owe ten dinars except a garment," or "ten garments except a dinar," the exception is not valid, and the confessor is bound by the entire sum. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: the exception from other than the genus is not valid, and the confessor is bound by the whole of what he acknowledged.

The proof for al-Shafi'i's position is that the word of exception is used both for the same genus and for a different genus. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor sinful speech, / Except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 206], so He excepted "peace" from the totality of idle talk. Similar to it is: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together, / Except Iblis﴾, and Iblis was of the totality of the angels. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [see p. 419 of this volume]. The poet said:

And a land in which there is no companion, / Except the yi'afir and except the 'is

So he excepted the yi'afir, which are the males of the gazelles, and the 'is, which are the white camels, from "companion" (anis). Similar to it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

I swore an oath without any reservation, / And there is no knowledge except a good opinion of a companion.

(The author, may Allah have mercy on him, did not mention the saying of al-Nabigha, or perhaps it fell from the copyist. It seems he is pointing to his saying: [the verse above]. This verse was cited by Sibawayh in his book as evidence for the accusative of what follows illa in disconnected exception, because good opinion is not of the category of knowledge. Al-mathnawiyya: the exception in an oath. The meaning: I swore my oath without making an exception in it, and my good opinion of my companion stood in my place as the knowledge that necessitates the oath. See Sibawayh's book.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 32–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Iblis, what is it with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ That is, what is it that prevents you?

(That you are not among those who prostrate.) That is, in not being.

(He said: "I would not prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered and molded.") He made clear his arrogance and envy, and that he was better than him, since he was from fire, and fire consumes clay, as its explanation has already been mentioned in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 170.]].

(He said: "Then get out of it.") That is, out of the heavens, or out of the Garden of Eden, or out of the company of the angels.

(For you are accursed.) That is, stoned with meteors. It was also said: cursed and ill-omened. All of this has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf.

(And indeed, upon you is the curse.) That is, My curse, as in Surah Sad [[See vol. 15, p. 228]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 36–38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ This request from Iblis was not out of confidence on his part in his standing with Allah, the Exalted, nor that he deserved to have his supplication answered. Rather, he asked for the postponement of his punishment as an increase in his trial, like the action of one who has despaired of safety. By his request for reprieve until the Day they are resurrected, he intended that he would not die, because on the Day of Resurrection there is no death, nor after it.

(﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those reprieved."﴾) meaning, among those given respite until a appointed time. Ibn Abbas said: "He meant by it the first blast" (al-nafkhah al-ula), i.e., the time when creation dies. It was also said: it is the known time which Allah has kept to His own knowledge and which Iblis is ignorant of. So Iblis will die and then be resurrected. Allah, the Exalted, said: "Everyone upon it will perish" (see vol. 17, p. 164). Regarding Allah's speech to him there are two views: first, that He spoke to him through His Messenger; second, that He spoke to him as a severe warning, not in a manner of honor or nearness.
