Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 39:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth"﴾. The meaning of ighwa (misguidance, leading astray) and zeenah (adornment, beautification) has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, pp. 174 and 195.]]. His beautifying here can take two forms: either by committing sins, or by preoccupying them with the adornments of this world so that they neglect obedience. The meaning of ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ is: I will surely lead them astray from the path of guidance.

Ibn Lahi'a, Abdullah, narrated from Darraj Abu al-Samh, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Iblis said, 'O my Lord, by Your might and Your majesty, I will not cease to mislead the children of Adam as long as their souls are within their bodies.' The Lord said, 'By My might and My majesty, I will not cease to forgive them as long as they seek My forgiveness.'"

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on surah 15, verse 40:

The people of Medina and the people of Kufa recited it with a fatha on the lam (al-mukhlaṣīn), meaning those whom You have chosen and purified (istakhlaṣtahum wa-akhlaṣtahum). The rest of the reciters read it with a kasra on the lam (al-mukhliṣīn), meaning those who have made their worship sincere to You, free from corruption or ostentation (riyā').

Abu Thumama related that the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) asked ʿIsa (peace be upon him) about those who are sincere to God, and he said: "The one who acts and does not like to be praised by people."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 41:

Ibn al-Khattab (ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him) said: its meaning is that this is a path that leads its follower straight until it brings him right to Paradise. Al-Hasan said: "ʿalayya" means "ilayya" (to me). Mujahid and al-Kisa'i said: this is in the sense of warning and threat, like your saying to someone you are threatening: "your path is upon me and your destination is to me." And like His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 50.]]. So the meaning of the statement is: this is a path whose return is to Me, so I will recompense each one for his deeds, meaning the path of worship. It was also said: the meaning is "upon Me" to indicate the straight path by clear explanation and proof. And it was said: by granting success and guidance. Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, al-Hasan, Qays ibn ʿAbbad, Abu Raja', Humayd and Ya'qub read ﴿This is a path, ʿaliyyun mustaqim﴾ with the ʿ"Aliyy" in the nominative and with tanwin, and its meaning is: elevated and straight, i.e., elevated in religion and truth. It was also said: elevated so that it is not reached, straight so that it is not deviated from.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 42:

The First Issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾. The scholars said: this means over their hearts. Ibn 'Uyayna said: that is, in causing them to fall into a sin that would deprive them of My pardon and constrict it for them. And these are those whom Allah guided, chose, selected and favoured.

I say: Perhaps someone will say: Allah has informed us about the attribute of Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, with His saying: ﴿So Satan caused them to slip﴾ [see vol. 1 p. 11, p. 321 and vol. 4 p. 24], and about a group of the companions of His Prophet with His saying: ﴿Satan only caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾ [see vol. 4 p. 243]. The answer is what has been mentioned, namely that he has no authority over their hearts or the place of their faith, and he does not cast them into a sin that leads to non-acceptance [in another copy: the pardon], rather repentance removes it and return (awba) erases it. The departure of Adam was not a punishment for what he committed, as has been explained earlier in al-Baqara [see vol. 1 p. 11, p. 321 and vol. 4 p. 24]. As for the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, the discussion about them has passed in Al 'Imran [see vol. 4 p. 243].

Then, His saying, glorified is He: "You have no authority over them" may be specific to those whom Allah protects, and it may be general for most times and states. His authority may also bring relief from distress and removal of grief, as happened with Bilal, when Satan came to him and lulled him as a child is lulled until he slept, and the Prophet ﷺ and his companions slept too, and they did not wake until the sun rose. They were alarmed and said: "What is the expiation for what we did through our negligence in our prayer?" The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "There is no negligence in sleep," and so their distress was relieved.

(Except those among the misguided who follow you) That is, the astray, the polytheists. That is, his authority is over these; the evidence is His saying: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [see p. 175 of this part].

The Second Issue: This verse and the one before it are evidence for the permissibility of excepting the few from the many and the many from the few, such as saying: "Ten except a dirham," or saying: "Ten except nine." Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: it is not permissible to except more than half or less. As for excepting the majority from the whole, it is not valid. Our evidence is this verse, for in it there is an exception of "the misguided" from "the servants" and "the servants" from "the misguided," and that indicates that excepting the lesser part from the whole and excepting the greater part from the whole are both permissible.

**Qur'an 15:43–44**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾. He means Iblis and whoever follows him.

(﴿It has seven gates﴾) meaning levels, one level above another. (﴿For each gate there is a portion of them, allotted﴾) meaning a known share.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Ibrahim Abu Harun al-Ghanawi informed us, saying: I heard Hittan ibn Abdullah al-Raqashi say: I heard Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "Do you know what the gates of Hell are like?" We said: "They are like our gates." He said: "No, they are like this, some above others." Al-Tha'labi added: and he placed one of his hands upon the other. "And Allah placed the Gardens upon the earth, and the Fires one above another. The lowest of them is Jahannam, above it al-Hutama, above it Saqar, above it al-Jahim, above it Laza, above it al-Sa'ir, and above it al-Hawiyah. Each gate is seventy times hotter than the one next to it."

I say: This is how this tafsir is reported. But most scholars hold that Jahannam is the highest of the levels (darakat), and that it is reserved for the disobedient of the Community of Muhammad ﷺ. It is the one that is emptied of its people, so the winds slam its gates. Then Laza, then al-Hutama, then Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah.

Al-Dahhak said: "In the highest level are the Muhammadans; in the second, the Christians; in the third, the Jews; in the fourth, the Sabians; in the fifth, the Magians; in the sixth, the polytheists of the Arabs; and in the seventh, the hypocrites, the family of Pharaoh, and whoever disbelieved among the people of the Table (al-Ma'ida)." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ (this has already been discussed in Surah al-Nisa'). [See vol. 4, p. 424.] He also said: ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment﴾. [See vol. 15, p. 318.] And He said: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment that I will not inflict upon anyone else in the worlds﴾. [See vol. 6, p. 368.]

Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, divided the evil scholars of this Community into categories corresponding to those gates. We mentioned this in our book al-Tadhkira.

Al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Jahannam has seven gates. One gate is for those who draw their sword against my Community." He said: "It is a gharib hadith."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "Jahannam has seven gates, one of which is for the Haruriyya" (the Kharijites). [In al-Durr al-Manthur by al-Suyuti: "Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'The martyr has a light, and whoever fights the Haruriyya has ten lights.' He used to say: 'Jahannam has seven gates: one of them is for the Haruriyya.' He said: 'They went out in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him.'"]

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Between every two gates is a distance of seventy years, and each gate is seventy times hotter than the one above it." We have mentioned all of this in the book al-Tadhkira.

Salam al-Tawil narrated from Abu Sufyan, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a portion of them, allotted﴾: "A portion for those who associated partners with Allah, a portion for those who doubted Allah, a portion for those who were heedless of Allah, a portion for those who preferred their desires over Allah, a portion for those who quenched their rage with the anger of Allah, a portion for those who turned their desire toward their share from Allah, and a portion for those who transgressed against Allah."

This was mentioned by al-Halimi Abu Abdullah al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan in his book Minhaj al-Din, and he said: "If this is established, then the polytheists (mushrikun) are the Thanawiyya (dualists) [in another copy: al-Wathaniyya (idolaters)]. The doubters are those who do not know whether they have a god or not, and who doubt whether His law is from Him or not. Those heedless of Allah are those who deny Him altogether and do not affirm Him; they are the Dahriyya (materialists who deny a Creator). Those who prefer their desires over Allah are those who are immersed in sins, because they deny the messengers of Allah and His command and prohibition. Those who quench their rage with the anger of Allah are those who kill the prophets of Allah and all who call to Him, and who torment anyone who advises them or follows a path other than theirs. Those who turn their desire toward their share from Allah are those who deny resurrection and reckoning; they worship what they desire, and they have their entire share from Allah, the Exalted. And those who transgress against Allah are those who do not care whether what they are in is true or false, so they do not reflect, do not take heed, and do not reason."

And Allah knows best what His Messenger ﷺ intended, if the hadith is established.

It is related that Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, when he heard this verse ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾, fled for three days out of fear, unable to think. He was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who asked him. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, was this verse revealed: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾? By the One who sent you with the truth, it has cut my heart." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾.

Bilal said: The Prophet ﷺ was praying alone in the Mosque of Madinah when a Bedouin woman passed by him and prayed behind him without him knowing. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a portion of them, allotted﴾. The Bedouin woman fell unconscious. The Prophet ﷺ heard her collapse (wajbatuha) [al-wajba: the sound of a thing falling, heard like a thud]. **Qur'an 15:43–44**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾. He means Iblis and whoever follows him.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Ibrahim Abu Harun al-Ghanawi informed us, saying: I heard Hittan ibn Abdullah al-Raqashi say: I heard Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "Do you know what the gates of Hell are like?" We said: "They are like our gates." He said: "No, they are like this, some above others." Al-Tha'labi added: and he placed one of his hands upon the other. "And Allah placed the Gardens upon the earth, and the Fires one above another. The lowest of them is Jahannam, above it al-Hutama, above it Saqar, above it al-Jahim, above it Laza, above it al-Sa'ir, and above it al-Hawiyah. Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, divided the evil scholars of this Community into categories corresponding to those gates. We mentioned this in our book al-Tadhkira.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 45–46:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be within gardens and springs﴾, meaning those who guarded themselves against grave sins and shirk; "jannat" means orchards. "ʿUyun" (springs) refers to the four rivers: of water, wine, milk and honey. As for the springs mentioned in Surat al-Insan [[See vol. 19, pp. 123, 262, 140, 139.]]: camphor, ginger and salsabil; and in Surat al-Mutaffifin [[See vol. 19, pp. 123, 262, 140, 139.]]: tasnim. Their mention and their people will come, God willing. The ʿayn in "ʿuyun" is pronounced with a ḍamma (ʿuyūn) according to the original form, and with a kasra (ʿiyūn) out of consideration for the yā', and both have been read.. both have been read.

(Enter it in peace, secure) The reading of the majority is "udkhulūhā" with a wasl alif and a ḍamma on the kh, from dakhala yadkhulu, in the imperative. Its implied sense: it was said, "Enter it." Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Ruways from Yaʿqub read "udkhilūhā" with ḍamm on the tanwin, wasl alif and kasra on the kh, in the passive form, from adkhala, meaning God caused them to enter it. Their practice is to kasrat the tanwin in such cases as "bi-rahmatin udkhulū [[See vol. 7, p. 274.]] al-jannah" and similar, except that here they transferred the vowel of the hamza onto the tanwin, since it is an alif of qat'; but this involves a shift from kasra to ḍamma and then from ḍamma to kasra, which is heavy on the tongue. "Bi-salam" means with safety from every disease and calamity. It is also said: with a greeting from God to them.

(Secure) meaning safe from death, punishment, removal and cessation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The first thing that happens to the people of Paradise when they enter Paradise is that two springs are presented to them. They drink from one of the two springs, and God removes whatever rancor (ghill) was in their hearts. Then they enter the other spring and bathe in it, and their complexions become radiant, their faces become clear, and the radiance of bliss (nadrat al-naʿim) flows over them. Something similar is reported from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him.

ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said: It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAli and the Companions, meaning the rancor that existed between them in the Jahiliyyah. But the first view is more apparent, as indicated by the context of the verse.

ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, said: I hope that I, Talhah and al-Zubayr will be among these.

Al-ghill means resentment and enmity; the verb derived from it is ghalla, yaghillu. It is also said to derive from ghulul, which is theft from the spoils of war: ghalla, yaghullu. It is also said to derive from treachery: aghalla, yughillu. As the poet said:

[[The verse is by al-Namir ibn Abyat, concerning the mother of his children. The story of her is that her brother al-Harith ibn Tawlab, the chief of his people, raided the Banu Asad and took captive from them a woman called "Hamzah bint Nawfal," and gave her to his brother al-Namir. She was hateful to him, so he kept her until she settled down and bore him children. Then on some of her days she said to him: "I have longed for my family." a repayment for a treacherous one who is false to trust.

This has already been discussed in Al ʿImran.[[See vol. 4, p. 255.]]

(Brothers, facing one another on couches.) That is, none of them looks at the back of another, out of closeness and mutual affection, according to Mujahid and others. It is also said: the couches turn however they wish, so no one sees the back of another. It is also said: "facing one another" means the spouses turn toward them and they turn toward their spouses with affection. Sururin is the plural of sarir, like jadid and judud. It is also said that it comes from surur (joy), as if it were an elevated, prepared place for joy. The first view is more apparent. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 51–54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾. The guests of Abraham: they are the angels who gave him the good news of a son and of the destruction of the people of Lot. Their mention has already passed [[See vol. 9, p. 62, p. 64 onward, p. 375.]]. Abraham, peace be upon him, was called Abu al-Dayfan (father of guests), and his palace had four doors so that no one would pass him by. The guest is called "dayf" because he is brought near (udifa) to you and lodges with you. What is due of the rights of the guest in [Surah] Hud has already passed, and praise be to God.

(﴿When they entered upon him﴾) He used the plural for the report because "dayf" is a noun that applies to the singular, the plural, the dual, the masculine and the feminine, like "masdar". Dafahu and adafahu: he inclined him (amalahu). From it is the hadith, "when the sun inclines (tadif) toward setting." And "dayfufat" (ḍayfūfat) of the arrow: its deviation from the target or the shot, and "al-idafa" and the grammatical construct (al-nahwiyya).

(﴿They said, "Peace."﴾) That is, they greeted with a greeting of peace.

(﴿He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾) That is, frightened and afraid. He said this only after he had brought the calf near and saw that they were not eating, as has passed in Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 62, p. 64 onward, p. 375.]]. It is said: he denied the greeting, since the custom of greeting was not known in their lands.

(﴿They said, "Do not be afraid."﴾) That is, the angels said, "Do not fear."

(﴿Indeed, we give you good news of a boy who is ʿalīm﴾) That is, ḥalīm (forbearing) [[In another manuscript: ḥakīm (wise).]], said by Muqatil. But the majority said: ʿālim (knowing). He is Isaac.

(﴿He said, "Do you give me good news although old age has touched me? So of what do you give good news?"﴾) "An" here is masdariyya (verbal), meaning "upon the touching of old age to me and to my wife." It has been discussed in Hud and Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, p. 62, p. 64 onward, p. 375.]], where it is said: (﴿So of what do you give good news?﴾) is an interrogative of wonder. It is also said to be a genuine interrogative. Al-Hasan read "tūjal" with a damma on the taʾ. Al-Aʿmash read "bashartumūnī" without an alif, and Nafiʿ and Shayba read "tubashshirūnī" with a kasra on the nun and lightening, like "atuḥājjūnī," whose explanation has already passed [[See vol. 7, p. 28.]]. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read "tubashshirūnnī" with a kasra on the nun and shadda, its underlying form being "tubashshirūnanī," so the nun was assimilated into the nun. The rest read "tubashshirūna" with a fatha on the nun, without a pronoun suffix.

The reading of the majority is "min al-qani'in" (مِنَ الْقانِطِينَ) with an alif. Opening and vowelling the nun in "yaqnatu" are two dialects, both of which have been recited. It is also reported as "yaqnutu" with a damma. No form "qanata yaqnatu" (قَنَطَ يَقْنَطُ) is attested for it. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this.
i.e., the deniers who have strayed from the path of rectitude. He means that he considered a child unlikely because of his old age, not that he despaired of the mercy of God, exalted is He.

**First issue:** When Abraham (peace be upon him) knew that they were angels, since they had told him of something that goes beyond normal custom, namely the good news of a son, he said: ﴿What is your business, then?﴾ The *khatb* is a weighty matter, so the meaning is: what is your affair and concern, and what have you come for?

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾, that is, his followers and the people of his religion.

﴿We will surely save them﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *lamunjūhum* with a light form (*takhfīf*) from *anjā*. The rest read it with a doubled form (*tashdīd*) from *najjā*, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. *Al-tanjiyah* and *al-injā'* both mean rescue and deliverance.

*you do not know who will give birth."*

*Al-aghbār* are the remnants of milk.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 61–65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the messengers came to the family of Lot, he said, "Indeed, you are people unknown to me."﴾ That is, "I do not know you." It was also said: they were young men, and he saw their beauty and feared for them the temptation of his people, and this is the denial.

(They said, "Rather, we have come to you with that about which they used to doubt") That is, they doubted that it would descend upon them, and it is the punishment.

(And We have come to you with the truth) That is, with certainty. It was also said: with the punishment.

(And indeed, we are truthful) That is, regarding their destruction.

(So set out with your family in the darkness of the night) "This has been discussed in Hud" [[see vol. 9, p. 79.]].

(And follow behind them) That is, be behind them so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment.

(And let not any of you look back) They were forbidden to look back so that they would hasten in the journey and move far from the town before the morning overtook them. It was also said: the meaning is, let no one fall behind.

(And proceed to where you are commanded) Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, Syria. Muqatil said: that is, Safad, a village from the villages of Lot, and it has been mentioned earlier. It was also said that he went to the land of al-Khalil, to a place called al-Yaqin, and al-Yaqin was so named because when the messengers departed, Ibrahim accompanied them, and he said to Jibril: "From where will they be swallowed up?" He said: "From here," and marked out a boundary for him, and Jibril departed. When Lot came, he sat with Ibrahim, and they both awaited that punishment. When the earth shook, Ibrahim said: "I have become certain in Allah," and so it was named al-Yaqin (certainty).

(And We have come to you with the truth) That is, with certainty. It was also said: with the punishment.

(And indeed, we are truthful) That is, regarding their destruction.

(So set out with your family in the darkness of the night) "This has been discussed in Hud" [[see vol. 9, p. 79.]].

(And follow behind them) That is, be behind them so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment.

(And let not any of you look back) They were forbidden to look back so that they would hasten in the journey and move far from the town before the morning overtook them. It was also said: the meaning is, let no one fall behind.

(And proceed to where you are commanded) Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, Syria. Muqatil said: that is, Safad, a village from the villages of Lot, and it has been mentioned earlier. It was also said that he went to the land of al-Khalil, to a place called al-Yaqin, and al-Yaqin was so named because when the messengers departed, Ibrahim accompanied them, and he said to Jibril: "From where will they be swallowed up?" He said: "From here," and marked out a boundary for him, and Jibril departed. When Lot came, he sat with Ibrahim, and they both awaited that punishment. When the earth shook, Ibrahim said: "I have become certain in Allah," and so it was named al-Yaqin (certainty).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 72:

There are three issues in this.

**The first issue:** Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "All the exegetes (mufassirun) said that God, exalted is He, swore here by the life of Muhammad (ﷺ), to honour him, that his people from Quraysh were in their intoxication, wandering blindly (﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾), and in their bewilderment, hesitating." I say: Al-Qadi Iyad said the same: "The people of exegesis (ahl al-tafsir) agreed that this is an oath by God, majestic is His majesty, by the lifespan of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Its original form is with a damma on the ʿayn, from al-ʿumr (lifetime), but it was given a fatha because of frequent usage. Its meaning is "by your survival, O Muhammad." It was also said: "by your life." This is the utmost in glorification, the highest degree of honour and dignity.

Abu al-Jawza said: "God did not swear by the life of anyone other than Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is the most noble of creation in His sight."

Ibn al-Arabi said: "What prevents God, glory be to Him, from swearing by the life of Lot and bestowing upon him whatever honour He wills? Whatever favour God gives to Lot, He gives double its honour to Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is more honoured with God than him. Do you not see that He gave Abraham the status of close friend (khullah) and Moses the direct speech (taklim), and gave that same to Muhammad? So if He swears by the life of Lot, the life of Muhammad is higher. One should not move from one speech to another speech that has not been mentioned, without necessity."

I say: What he said is good, for God's oath by the life of Muhammad (ﷺ) would be a parenthetical statement (kalaman muʿtaridan) within the story of Lot. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr ʿAbd al-Rahim ibn ʿAbd al-Karim said in his tafsir: "It is possible to say that this refers to the people of Lot, meaning they were in their intoxication, wandering blindly." It was also said: when Lot admonished his people and said, "These are my daughters," the angels said: "O Lot, ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾," and they did not know what would befall them at dawn.

If it is said: God swore by the fig and the olive and Mount Sinai, so what is the point of this? It is said to him: Whatever God swears by is a proof of its superiority over what is counted in its category. Likewise, our Prophet (ﷺ) must be superior to those who are in his category.

*Al-ʿumr* and *al-ʿamr* (with a damma or fatha on the ʿayn) are two dialect forms with the same meaning, except that in oaths only the fatha is used, because of frequent usage. You say *ʿammarakallah*, meaning "I ask God to grant you long life." *Laʿamruka* is in the nominative (*marfuʿ*) because it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. The meaning is: "By your life, what I swear by is..."

**The second issue:** Many scholars disliked that a person says *laʿamri* (by my life), because its meaning is "by my life." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: "It is disliked for a man to say *laʿamri*, because it is an oath by one's own life, and that is the speech of weak men." Malik said something similar: "Weak men and effeminate men swear by your life and your livelihood. It is not the speech of men of strength (ahl al-dhukran). Even if God, glory be to Him, swore by it in this story, that is a demonstration of the nobility of rank and the elevation of his station, so it should not be applied to anyone else nor used for anything else."

Ibn Habib said: "*Laʿamruka* in speech should be restricted to this verse." Qatada said: "It is from the speech of the Arabs." Ibn al-Arabi said: "I too say this, but the Shariʿa has cut it off from usage and returned the oath to God." I say: The oath by *laʿamruka* and *laʿamri* and similar phrases is frequent in Arabic poetry and eloquent speech.

Al-Nabigha said:

*By my life, and my life is not light upon me,*
*the Aqarie have spoken falsehood against me.*
[He meant by *al-Aqarie* the Banu ʿAwf, who had reported on him to al-Nuʿman.]

Another poet said:

*By your life, death does not miss the youth,*
*it is like the stretched rope and its twisted strands in the hand.*
[The verse is by Tarafa ibn al-ʿAbd. *Al-Tawl* is the rope, and *thaniyahu* is what is twisted from it.]

Another poet said:

*O you who marry the Pleiades to Suhayl,*
*by your life, how can the two meet?*

Another poet said:

*If the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,*
*by God's life, their pleasure delights me.*

Some scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: "This is not permissible, because one does not say *ʿamr* for God; He is eternal (azali)." This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi.

**The third issue:** The discussion of what may be sworn by and what may not be sworn by has already passed in *al-Ma'ida* [see vol. 7, p. 269 and following]. There we mentioned the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal on one who swears by the Prophet (ﷺ): he is obliged to expiate (kaffarah).

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "Whoever permits swearing by other than God, of what is permissible to glorify with a right of some rights, does not say it is an oath that carries an expiation, except that whoever intends a lie is blameworthy, because inwardly he treats lightly what he is obliged to glorify."

They said: God's words *laʿamruka* mean "and your life." When God swears by the life of His Prophet, He intends to clarify for us that it is permissible for us to swear by his life. According to the school of Malik, the meaning of His words *laʿamruka*, *al-tini wa al-zaytun* [see vol. 20, pp. 110, 72, 59], *al-tur*, *wa kitabin masṭur* [see vol. 17, pp. 58, 81], *wa al-najmi idha hawa*, *wa al-shamsi wa duhaha* [see vol. 20, pp. 110, 72, 59], *la uqsimu bihadha al-balad*, *wa anta hillun bihadha al-balad*, *wa walidin wa ma walad* [see vol. 20, pp. 110, 72, 59], all of this means: "by the Creator of the fig and the olive, by the Lord of the inscribed Book, by the Lord of the city in which you dwell, by the Creator of your livelihood and your life, and by the right of Muhammad." The oath and the swearing are thus by Him, glory be to Him, not by the created.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "Whoever permits swearing by other than God interprets the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Do not swear by your fathers.' He said: 'He only forbade swearing by the fathers who were disbelievers. Do you not see that when they swore by their fathers, he said: ﴿Surely the mountain is more honoured with God than your fathers who died in the age of ignorance﴾?' Malik took the hadith according to its apparent meaning."

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "Those who permit it also argue that the oaths of Muslims have been in practice since the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until today, that they swear by the Prophet (ﷺ). Even today, when one of the people of Medina litigates against his companion, he says: 'Swear to me by the right of what this grave contains, and by the right of the one who dwells in this grave,' meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). Likewise, they swear by the Haram, the great sacred places, the Rukn and the Maqam, the Mihrab, and what is recited in it." [Consider this together with his words, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or keep silent."]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise﴾. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: at the time of the sunrising of the sun. It is said: "ashraqat al-shams" means it shone, and "sharaqat" means it rose. And it is said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. And "ashraqa al-qawm" means they entered the time of the sunrise, like "asbahu" (they entered the morning) and "amsaw" (they entered the evening), and this is what is meant in the verse. It is also said: he meant the breaking of dawn (shuruq al-fajr). It is also said: the beginning of the punishment was at dawn and it extended until the sunrise, so the complete destruction was at that time. And Allah knows best. And "al-Sayhah" (the Cry) is the punishment. The mention of "sijjil" has already passed [[See vol. 9, p. 81.]].

**Issue One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿for those who discern (al-mutawassimin)﴾. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated in *Nawadir al-Usul* from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "for those who look closely (lil-mutafarrisin)." This is also the view of Mujahid. Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Beware of the insight of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah," then he recited: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ He said: This is a *gharib* hadith.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: *lil-mutawassimin* means *lil-mutafakkirin* (those who reflect). Al-Dahhak said: *lil-nazzarin* (those who observe). The poet said [[It is Tarif ibn Tamim al-'Anbari (cited in the shawahid of Sibawayh)]]:

*Whenever a tribe arrives at 'Ukaz, they send to their 'arif (chief) to discern (yatawassamu).*

Qatadah said: *lil-mu'tabirin* (those who take lessons). Zuhair said:

*And in them is a pleasure for the friend, and a sight, delightful to the eye of the observer who discerns.*

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *lil-mutabassirin* (those who see clearly), and the meanings are close. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated from the hadith of Thabit, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has servants who know people through *tawassum*." The scholars said: *al-tawassum* (discerning by signs) is from the *wasm*, which is the mark by which one is guided to something other than itself. It is said: "I discerned goodness in him (tawassamtu fihi al-khayr)" when I saw the brand of that in him. From this is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah to the Prophet ﷺ:

*I have discerned in you goodness, which I recognize, and Allah knows that I have a steadfast sight.*

Another said:

*I discerned him when I saw his dignity upon him, and I said: "This man is of the family of Hashim."*

And *ittasama al-rajul* means when a man makes for himself a sign by which he is recognized. And *tawassama al-rajul* means he sought both marks. And he recited:

*And they became in the morning like tender palm-trees, at dawn, on a road of a departing traveler who was discerned (mutawassim).*

Tha'lab said: *al-wasim* is the one who looks at you from your head to your foot. The root of *tawassum* is firmness and reflection, derived from *al-wasm*, which is the impression made by an iron tool on the hide of a camel or other animal. This occurs through excellence of natural disposition, sharpness of insight, and clarity of thought. Others added: and emptying the heart of the filth of the world, and purifying it from the stains of sins, the turbidity of character, and the excesses of worldly life.

Nahshal narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning *lil-mutawassimin*: "For the people of righteousness and goodness." The Sufis claimed that it is a *karamah* (a gift of grace from Allah). It was said: Rather, it is *istidlal* (inference) by signs. Some signs appear clearly to everyone at first sight, and some are hidden, so they do not appear to everyone and are not perceived at first glance.

Al-Hasan said: "The *mutawassimun* are those who discern matters, so they know that He who destroyed the people of Lut is able to destroy the disbelievers. This is among the manifest proofs." Similar is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "No one asked me about anything without my knowing whether he was a jurist (faqih) or not a jurist."

It is narrated from al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that they were in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, and a man was at the door of the mosque. One of them said: "I think he is a carpenter (najjar)." The other said: "Rather, a blacksmith (haddad)." So those present rushed to the man and asked him, and he said: "I was a carpenter, and today I am a blacksmith."

It is narrated from Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali that he came upon a man who was reciting the Qur'an, and he stopped and said: "Whoever makes it heard, Allah will make him heard by it, and whoever shows off, Allah will expose him by it." We said to him: "It seems you are hinting at this man." He said: "This one recites the Qur'an to you today, and tomorrow he will go out as a Haruri (Kharijite)." He was indeed the head of the Harurites, and his name was Mirdas.

It is narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd entered upon him, and he said: "This is the chief of the youths of Basra, if he does not innovate." Then, regarding his affairs of *qadar* (predestination), what happened happened, until most of his brothers abandoned him. And [al-Hasan] said to Ayyub: "This is the chief of the youths of the people of Basra," and he did not make an exception.

It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said to Dawud al-Azdi while disputing with him: "You will not die until you are cauterized on your head," and so it was.

It is narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was visited by a group from Madhhij, among whom was al-Ashtar. He gazed intently at him and then said: "Who is this?" They said: "Malik ibn al-Harith." He said: "What is wrong with him? May Allah fight him! I see from him a grievous day for the Muslims." And what happened from him in the *fitnah* (strife) happened.

It is narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, that Anas ibn Malik entered upon him, and he had passed by the market and looked at a woman. When he looked at him, 'Uthman said: "One of you enters upon me while in his eyes is the trace of adultery." Anas said to him: "Is there revelation after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: "No, but it is proof, insight, and truthfulness."

Many similar reports are narrated from the Companions and the Followers, may Allah be pleased with them all.

**Issue Two:** The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "If it is established that *tawassum* and *tafarrus* (physiognomic insight) are among the means of perceiving meanings, then no ruling is based on it, and neither the one marked nor the one whose insight is read is held accountable by it. The Shafi'i (or Maliki) Qadi al-Qudat in Baghdad, during my time in Syria, used to judge by physiognomy in rulings, following the method of Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah when he was a judge. Our shaykh, Fakhr al-Islam Abu Bakr al-Shashi, wrote a booklet refuting him, which he wrote for me in his own hand and gave to me, and that is correct. For the sources of rulings are known by the Law and perceived with certainty, and physiognomy is not among them."

This passage is Qurtubi's commentary on Qur'an 15:76–79.

Al-Hijr has several meanings. One of them is the Hijr of the Kaaba. Another is "the forbidden," as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and a forbidden barrier﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 58], meaning, forbidden and prohibited. Al-hijr also means the intellect, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿for those of understanding﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 42]. Al-hijr also means the placket of a shirt, though the fatha is more eloquent. Al-hijr also means a female horse. And al-Hijr means the dwellings of Thamud, which is what is meant here, that is, the town. Al-Azhari said: Qatadah said: it is the area between Makkah and Tabuk, the valley in which Thamud lived. Al-Tabari said: it is a land between the Hijaz and al-Sham, and they were the people of Salih. He said: ﴿the messengers﴾, though it was Salih alone, but whoever denies one prophet has denied all the prophets, because they share one religion in its fundamentals, so it is not permissible to differentiate between them. It has also been said: they denied Salih and those who followed him and those prophets who came before him as well. And Allah knows best.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Umar that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ descended at al-Hijr during the Battle of Tabuk, he commanded them not to drink from its well nor draw water from it. They said: "We have kneaded dough and drawn water." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pour out the water and to throw away that dough.

In the Sahih, from Ibn Umar: the people stopped with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at al-Hijr, the land of Thamud, and they drew water from its wells and kneaded dough with it. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to pour out what they had drawn, and to feed the dough to the camels, and he commanded them to draw water from the well that the she-camel used to come to.

It is also narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: We passed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by al-Hijr, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." Then he urged his mount and hastened on.

I say: In this verse, whose ruling the Lawgiver has explained and whose matter he has clarified, there are eight issues which the scholars have derived, and the jurists have differed regarding some of them.

The first: the reprehensibility of entering those places. Some scholars applied to this the entering of the graves of the disbelievers. If a person enters any of those places and graves, he should do so in the manner the Prophet ﷺ guided to: with reflection, fear, and haste.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not enter the land of Babylon, for it is cursed."

Issue: The Prophet commanded that what they had drawn from the well of Thamud be poured out, and that what had been kneaded and baked with it be thrown away, because it is water of divine wrath, so it was not permissible to benefit from it, fleeing from the wrath of Allah. And he said: "Feed it to the camels."

I say: This is also the ruling for impure water and what is kneaded with it.

The second: Malik said: what is not permissible to use of food and drink is permissible to feed to camels and animals, since they are not under obligation. Similarly he said regarding impure honey: it may be fed to bees.

The third: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that the dough kneaded with this water be fed to the camels, and did not command its disposal, as he commanded regarding the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar. This indicates that the flesh of donkeys is more severe in prohibition and more serious in rendering things impure. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that the earnings of the cupper be fed to the water-camel and the slaves, and that was neither because of prohibition nor impurity. Al-Shafi'i said: Had it been forbidden, he would not have ordered that it be fed to his slaves, for he is accountable for it just as he is accountable for himself.

The fourth: his ﷺ command to feed the camels the kneaded dough is evidence for the permissibility of a man carrying an impurity to his dogs so that they may eat it, contrary to those among our companions who forbade this and said: dogs are not to be fed impurities, and one should not carry them to them.

The fifth: his ﷺ command that they draw water from the she-camel's well is evidence for seeking blessing from the traces of the prophets and the righteous, even if their eras have long passed and their traces have faded. Just as in the first point there is evidence regarding the people of corruption and the blameworthiness of their dwellings and traces. This is so, although the verified position is that inanimate things are not held accountable; yet what is associated with the beloved is beloved, and what is associated with the disliked and hated is hated, as Kuthayyir said:

I love, for love of her, the blacks, until
I love, for love of her, the black dogs.

And as another said:

I pass by the dwellings, the dwellings of Layla,
I kiss this wall and that wall.

And those dwellings—they did not captivate my heart,
but it is love of the one who dwelt in them that did.

And the sixth: some scholars forbade prayer in this place, saying: "Prayer is not valid in it, because it is an abode of wrath and a spot of anger." Ibn al-'Arabi said: This place is thus excepted from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification" (tahur). So it is not permissible to perform tayammum with its dust, nor to perform wudu' with its water, nor to pray in it.

At-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade prayer in seven places: in the dunghill, the slaughterhouse, the graveyard, the middle of the road, the bathhouse, the camel pens, and above the House of Allah. There are also reports on this subject from Abu Marthad, Jabir and Anas. The hadith of Ibn 'Umar has an isnad that is not very strong, and Zayd ibn Jubayrah has been criticised regarding his memorisation.

Our scholars have added: the usurped house, the church, the synagogue, a house in which there are images, a usurped land, or a place in front of which one would be facing a sleeping person, or a man's face, or a wall upon which there is najasah. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Among these places, some are forbidden because of the right of another person, some because of the right of Allah the Exalted, and some because of certain (muhaqqaqah) or predominant najasah. As for what is forbidden because of najasah: if a clean cloth is spread in it, as in the bathhouse and the graveyard, either within it or facing it, then that is permissible according to al-Mudawwanah. Abu Mus'ab reported from him (Malik) a dislike (of this). Our scholars distinguished between an old graveyard and a new one with respect to najasah, and between the graveyard of the Muslims and that of the polytheists, because the latter is an abode of punishment and a spot of wrath, like al-Hijr.

Malik said in al-Majmu'ah: One should not pray in the camel pens even if one spreads a cloth, as though he saw two reasons for it: concealment (istitar) by them [[In the Muwatta': "because one is concealed by them for urination and defecation, so the places where camels rest are hardly safe from najasah."]] and their skittishness (nifar), which spoils the prayer for the one praying. If there is only one camel [[i.e., a single she-camel.]], there is no harm, as the Prophet ﷺ used to do, according to the sahih hadith. Malik also said: One should not pray on a rug that has images in it, except out of necessity. Ibn ... disliked praying facing the qiblah where there are images, and in a usurped house; if one did so, it suffices him. Some of them reported from Malik that prayer in a usurped house is not valid. Ibn al-'Arabi said: In my view, this differs from the land, for a house is not entered except with permission, whereas land, even if it is owned, retains its character as a place of mosque-ness, which ownership does not nullify. I say: the correct view, if Allah wills, which reason and tradition indicate, is that prayer in every clean place is permissible and valid. As for what is narrated from his saying ﷺ: "This is a valley in which there is a devil," it was transmitted by Ma'mar from al-Zuhri, who said: "And leave the place in which heedlessness has befallen you." And the saying of 'Ali: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade me to pray in the land of Babylon, for it is cursed. And his peace be upon him saying when he passed by al-Hijr of Thamud: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping." And his prohibition of prayer in camel pens, along with that which is in this chapter, is referred back to the established principles and the sound proofs. The Imam, the memoriser Abu 'Umar said: The view we prefer in this chapter is that this valley and other places on earth are permissible for prayer in all of them, so long as there is no certain najasah preventing it. There is no sense in the argument of those who argue that the place of sleep is a place to be avoided for prayer, a place of the devil, a cursed place where prayer should not be established. Everything that has been related in this chapter about the prohibition of prayer in the graveyard, in the land of Babylon, in camel pens and other such matters, all of that, in our view, is abrogated (mansukh) and rejected in favour of the generality of his saying ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me entirely a mosque and a means of purification," and his saying ﷺ, informing that this is among his virtues and among what he was specially favoured with. His virtues, according to the people of knowledge, are not subject to abrogation, alteration or diminution. He ﷺ said: "I have been given five [it has been related as six, and as three and four, and they reach more than nine [[In Uwwi.]]], which none before me was given: I was sent to the red and the black; I was supported with awe; the spoils were made lawful for me; the earth was made for me a mosque and a means of purification; I was given intercession; I was sent with comprehensive words; while I was sleeping, the keys of the earth were brought to me and placed in my hand; I was given al-Kawthar; and the prophets were sealed with me." This was related by a group of the Companions, some of them mentioning some of these and others mentioning what others did not, and all of them are sound. Increase in his virtues is permissible, but diminution in them is not. Do you not see that he was a servant before he was a prophet, then he was a prophet before he was a messenger, and so it has been related from him? And he said: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you," then there was revealed: "That Allah may forgive you what is past of your sin and what is to come." [[See vol. 16 p. 261.]] He heard a man say: "O best of creation," and he said: "That is Ibrahim." And he said: "None of you should say, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" And he said: "The master Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, upon them be peace." Then after all of that he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting." So his virtues ﷺ continued to increase until Allah took him. From this we say: it is not permissible for them to be abrogated, nor to be exempted, nor diminished, and increase in them is permissible. And by his saying ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification," we permitted prayer in the graveyard, the bathhouse, and in every place on earth provided it is clean of impurities. He ﷺ said to Abu Dharr: "Wherever prayer overtakes you, pray, for the whole earth is a mosque," which al-Bukhari mentioned, and he did not single out one place from another. As for those who argued with the hadith of Ibn Wahb, who said: Yahya ibn Ayyub informed me from Zayd ibn Jubayrah from Dawud ibn Husayn from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, the hadith of at-Tirmidhi which we mentioned, it is a hadith in which Zayd ibn Jubayrah stands alone, and they rejected it from him. This hadith is not known as musnad except through the narration of Yahya ibn Ayyub from Zayd ibn Jubayrah. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd wrote to 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi', the client of Ibn 'Umar, asking him about this hadith, and 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi' wrote back to him: "I do not know who related this from Nafi' except that he has spoken falsehood against him." Al-Halwani related it from Sa'id ibn Abi Maryam from al-Layth, and there is in it no specification of the graveyard of the polytheists from others. It has also been related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib who said: My beloved ﷺ forbade me to pray in the graveyard, and forbade me to pray in the land of Babylon, for it is cursed. Its isnad is weak, agreed upon as weak; and Abu Salih, who related it from 'Ali, is Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghifari, a Basran who is not well known, and his hearing from 'Ali is not sound, and those below him are unknown and not identified. Abu 'Umar said: In this chapter, concerning 'Ali, from his own saying and not raised to the Prophet, there is a hadith of good isnad, related by al-Fadl ibn Dukayn who said: al-Mughirah ibn Abi al-Hurr al-Kindi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-'Anbas Hujr ibn 'Anbas narrated to me, saying: We went out with 'Ali to the Harurites, and when we passed Suriya and reached the land of Babylon, we said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the time has come, the prayer, the prayer!" But he refused to speak to anyone. They said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the time has come." He said: "Yes, but I will not pray in a land which Allah has caused to sink." Al-Mughirah ibn Abi al-Hurr was a trustworthy Kufan, so said Yahya ibn Ma'in and others. Hujr ibn 'Anbas was among the senior companions of 'Ali. At-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The whole earth is a mosque except the graveyard and the bathhouse." At-Tirmidhi said: Sufyan al-Thawri related it from 'Amr ibn Yahya from his father from the Prophet ﷺ as a mursal, and it seems to be more established and sounder. Abu 'Umar said: So the argument from it falls away for those who do not hold mursal to be a proof; and even if it were established, the correct understanding is what we have mentioned. We do not say, as some of the adherents of the Madinan school said, that the graveyard in this hadith and others is meant specifically as the graveyard of the polytheists, for he said: "the graveyard and the bathhouse" with the definite article, so it is not permissible to restrict that to one graveyard rather than another, or one bathhouse rather than another, without a revealed text on it. This is a view for which there is no proof from the Book, nor the Sunnah, nor a sound report, and it has no place in analogy or reasoning, nor does the implication of the address indicate it, nor did the report come out for it. The specification of the graveyard of the polytheists by those who single it out must be one of two things: either because of the polytheists' coming and going to it on foot, in which case there is no sense in singling out the graveyard by mention, for every place where they are in body and foot is the same; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is too exalted to speak without meaning. Or it is because it is a spot of wrath, in which case the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not have built his mosque in the graveyard of the polytheists, dug it up, levelled it and built upon it. And if it were permissible for someone to single out one graveyard from the general category for prayer, the graveyard of the polytheists would be the more fitting for specification and exception on the basis of this hadith. Everyone who disliked prayer in the graveyard did not single out one graveyard from another, because the definite article indicates the genus, not a specific known one. And if there were a distinction between the graveyard of the Muslims and that of the polytheists, the Prophet ﷺ would have explained it and would not have left it out, for he was sent as one to make clear. If it were acceptable for an ignorant person to say "the graveyard of such-and-such," it would be permissible for another to say "the bathhouse of such-and-such," since the hadith says "the graveyard and the bathhouse." Likewise his saying "the dunghill and the slaughterhouse": it is not permissible to say "the dunghill of such-and-such," nor "the slaughterhouse of such-and-such," nor "the road of such-and-such," for arbitrary judgement in the religion of Allah is not permissible. The scholars agreed that tayammum on the graveyard of the polytheists is permissible if the place is good, pure, clean. Likewise they agreed that whoever prayed in

the church or the monastery, on a clean spot, his prayer is valid and permissible. This has already been discussed in the surah "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 255.]]. It is known that a church is more likely to be a place of wrath than a graveyard, because it is a place where God is disobeyed and disbelieved in, whereas a graveyard is not like that. The Sunnah has indeed come with the taking of churches and synagogues as mosques. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Talq ibn Ali, who said: "We went out as a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ, pledged allegiance to him, prayed with him, and informed him that in our land there was a church (bai'ah) of ours," and he mentioned the hadith. In it: "When you return to your land, break your church and take it as a mosque." Abu Dawud mentioned, from Uthman ibn Abi al-As, that the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to make the mosque of al-Ta'if where their idols (tawaghit) had been. This was also discussed in "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 254 and beyond.]]. And sufficient for you is the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ, which was founded upon piety, built in the graveyard of the polytheists, and it is a proof against everyone who disliked praying in it. Among those who disliked praying in a graveyard, whether it belonged to Muslims or polytheists, was al-Thawri, who held that if one prays in a graveyard in a place free of impurity, the prayer is valid, due to the well-known hadiths on this matter, and due to the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Pray in your houses and do not make them graves," and due to the hadith of Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Do not pray towards graves, and do not sit upon them." These are two hadiths that are sound in their chain of narration, but there is no proof in them, because they admit of interpretation, and one is not required to refrain from praying in every clean place except on the basis of a proof that admits of no interpretation. No jurist among the Muslims distinguished between the graveyard of Muslims and that of polytheists, except for the erroneous opinion we have related, which is not worth occupying oneself with, and which has no basis in sound reasoning or authentic transmission. And the eighth [[He means the eighth of the issues derived by jurists. The hā'iṭ is the garden.]]: the garden (ha'it) in which filth and dung are thrown for manuring, so one does not pray in it until it has been watered three times, due to what al-Daraqutni narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning a garden in which dung and filth are thrown, that he said: "When it has been watered three times, pray in it." He also narrated it from the hadith of Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that he was asked about these walls into which dung and this manure are thrown, whether one may pray in them. He said: "When they have been watered three times, pray in them." This was attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. They differed regarding the chain of narration, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 81:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾, meaning: by Our signs, as in His saying: "Bring us our morning meal" (ātinā ghadā'anā), meaning: bring us our food. [See vol. 11, p. 12.] The intended sign is the she-camel, and there were in her many signs: her emerging from the rock, the nearness of her birth at the time of her emergence, her great size such that no camel resembled her, and the abundance of her milk, enough for all of them. It is possible that Salih had other signs besides the she-camel, such as the well and other things.

(But they were ﴿turning away from them﴾), meaning: they did not take heed.

The word *al-nahtu* (carving) in the language of the Arabs means shaping and hollowing out. One says *nahata-hu yanhitu-hu* (with a kasra on the ha, and with a fatha, which is how al-Hasan recited it; the one who wrote on the three-vowel variants (*al-muthallathat*) said that the widely transmitted (*mutawatir*) reading is the sound one) *nahtan*, meaning he shaped it. *Al-nuhatah* is the shavings, and *al-minhat* is the tool with which it is carved. In the revelation: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ (37:95), meaning, you hew and make. They used to take houses for themselves out of the mountains, owing to the great strength they possessed. [[See vol. 15, p. 96.]]

(*Amin*) means safe from the fear that they might fall upon them or that the houses might collapse. It is said: *aminin* from death. It is said: from the punishment.

(﴿Then the Cry seized them at dawn.﴾) means at the time of morning, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). The Cry has already been mentioned in Surah Hud and Surah al-A'raf. [[See vol. 9, p. 61 and vol. 7, p. 242.]]

(﴿So what they had earned did not avail them.﴾) of wealth and of fortresses in the mountains, nor what they had been given of strength.

The word *al-nahtu* (carving) in the language of the Arabs means shaping and hollowing out. Scholars differed concerning "the seven oft-repeated" (al-sab' al-mathani). It was said that it is al-Fatihah (the Opening chapter). This was the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayrah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Hasan and others. It has also been related from the Prophet ﷺ through reliable channels, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla. This has already been discussed in the tafsir of al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 108.]]. al-Tirmidhi transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Al-hamdu lillah (All praise is for Allah) is Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), and al-sab' al-mathani (the seven oft-repeated)." He said: This is a hasan sahih hadith (a good, sound hadith). This is an explicit text, and it has already been mentioned in the discussion of al-Fatihah. The poet said:

I adjure you by the One who sent down the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, the seven of the oft-repeated.

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the seven long (surahs): al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal and al-Tawbah together, since there is no basmalah between them. al-Nasa'i related: 'Ali ibn Hujr told us, Shurayk told us, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic: (seven of the oft-repeated). He said: The seven long ones. It was called mathani because the lessons, the rulings and the limits are repeated (thuniyyat) within them. Some people denied this and said: This verse was revealed in Makkah, and none of the long surahs had been revealed at that time. It was answered that Allah, Exalted, sent down the Qur'an to the lowest heaven all at once and then sent it down from there in installments. So what He sent down to the lowest heaven is as if it had been given to Muhammad ﷺ, even if it had not yet been revealed to him. Among those who said that they are the seven long ones were 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Jarir said:

May Allah reward al-Farazdaq, when evening comes, for neglecting al-Mufassal and al-Mathani.

It was also said: al-mathani is the whole Qur'an. Allah, Exalted, said: "A Book consistent, oft-repeated (mutashabihan mathani)" [[See vol. 15, p. 248.]]. This is the view of al-Dahhak, Tawus and Abu Malik, and Ibn 'Abbas also said it. It was said that it is called mathani because the reports and stories are repeated (thuniyyat) in it. Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib said in elegy for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

He was a shining light by which one is guided, singled out by the revelation of the oft-repeated, the Exalted.

That is, the Qur'an. It was also said: The seven oft-repeated refers to the divisions of the Qur'an: commands, prohibitions, glad tidings, warnings, parables, enumeration of blessings, and reports of past generations. This was said by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam. The correct view is the first, because it is an explicit text. We have already mentioned in the discussion of al-Fatihah that calling it mathani does not prevent calling something else by that name; however, when a clear text from the Prophet ﷺ is established that admits no interpretation, one must stop at it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Great Qur'an﴾. There is an implied element in it, its estimation being: that al-Fatihah is the Great Qur'an, because it includes what relates to the foundations of Islam. This has already been discussed in al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 112.]]. It was also said: the waw (and) is superfluous (muqhamah), and the meaning is: "And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the Great Qur'an." From this is the poet's saying:

To the noble king and the son of the brave warrior, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

This has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 213.]].

There are two issues.

The first concerns His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾. The meaning is: "I have made you sufficient with the Qur'an, above what is in the hands of people. Indeed, he is not of us who does not *yataghanna* (find sufficiency) in the Qur'an." That is, he is not of us who thinks that what he has of the Qur'an does not suffice him, so that his gaze reaches out to the adornments of this world while he possesses the knowledge of his Lord (al-Mawla). It is said that seven caravans came from Basra and Adhri'at to the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir on a single day, carrying wheat, perfume, jewels, and merchandise of the sea. The Muslims said: "If these goods were ours, we would strengthen ourselves with them and spend them in the way of God." So God the Exalted revealed: "And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]," meaning that these are better for you than the seven caravans, so do not extend your eyes toward them. Ibn 'Uyayna held this view, and he cited the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He is not of us who does not *yatagharran* (find sufficiency) in the Qur'an," meaning, he who does not find sufficiency in it. This meaning has already been mentioned at the beginning of the book.[[راجع ج ١ ص ١٢.]] The meaning of ﴿pairs of them﴾ is: likenesses in blessings, that is, the rich are like one another in wealth, and so they are pairs.

The second issue: this verse requires warning against constantly yearning for the goods of this world and against the servant turning his attention to the worship of his Lord. Similar to it is the verse: ﴿And do not extend your eyes to what We have given to pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them therein﴾.[[راجع ج ١١ ص ٢٦١.]] This is not the case, for it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There has been made beloved to me of your world women and perfume, and the coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer."[[كذا في سنن النسائي ومسند الامام أحمد. والذي في الأصول: "حبب إلى من دنياكم ثلاث ... إلخ" وبكلمة "ثلاث" لا يستقيم الكلام. راجع كشف الخفا ج ١ ص ٣٣٨ ففيه بحث شيق واف.]] The Prophet (peace be upon him) would occupy himself with women, as is the natural disposition of humankind and the inclination of human creation, and he would take care to use perfume. The coolness of his eye was found only in prayer, at the time of intimate conversation with his Lord, and he regarded that intimate conversation as more fitting and more deserving than those things. There was not in the religion of Muhammad *rahbaniyya* (monasticism) or complete devotion to righteous deeds to the exclusion of all else, as there was in the religion of 'Isa (Jesus).[[أي الانقطاع الكلى عن الدنيا فإنه من معاني الرهبانية.]]

God, glory be to Him, prescribed the *hanifiyya* (the pure, upright monotheistic way), tolerant, free of hardship, and light upon the human being, who takes from his humanity its desires and returns to God with a sound heart. Al-Farra' and the sincere among the virtuous held that abstaining from pleasures and devoting oneself wholly to the Lord of the earth and the heavens is preferable today, because the unlawful has prevailed over this world, and the servant is compelled in earning his livelihood to mix with those with whom mixing is not permissible and to deal with those with whom dealing is forbidden. Thus seclusion is better, and fleeing from this world is more correct and more just for the servant. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There will come a time upon people when the best wealth of a Muslim will be sheep, which he herds to the mountain peaks and the places of rain, fleeing with his religion from trials."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾: that is, do not grieve over the polytheists if they do not believe. It was also said: the meaning is, do not grieve over what they have been given enjoyment of in this world, for you have in the Hereafter something better than it. It was also said: do not grieve over them if they go to the punishment, for they are people of the punishment.

﴿And lower your wing for the believers﴾: that is, soften your side toward those who have believed in you, and be humble toward them. The origin of this is that when a bird gathers its chick to itself, it spreads its wing and then folds it over the chick. So this was made a description of a person's drawing close to his followers. It is said: "So-and-so is *khafid al-janah*," meaning dignified and calm. The two wings of a son of Adam are his two sides, and from this comes the verse: ﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾.[[راجع ج ١١ ص ١٩٠.]] The wing of a bird is its arm. The poet said:

*And it is enough for you that the young men of a chief of a people
Extend a wing over a brother who is ill.*

That is, humility and gentleness.

In the speech there is an ellipsis: that is, "I am the plain warner of a punishment," so the object was omitted, since the warning itself points to it, as He said in another place: ﴿I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 346.]]. It has been said: the kāf is extra, meaning "I have warned you of what We sent down upon the muqtasimīn," as in His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 7.]]; "I have warned you of the like of what We sent down upon the muqtasimīn." It was also said: the meaning is "as We sent down upon the muqtasimīn," that is, of the punishment, and We have sufficed you against the mockers; so proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists who transgressed, for We have sufficed you against those chiefs from whom you were encountering what you encountered.

As for the muqtasimīn, there are seven opinions about them.

The first: Muqatil and al-Farra' said they were sixteen men whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughira sent out during the season of pilgrimage, and they divided among themselves the outskirts (aʿqāb) of Makkah, its mountain passes (anqāb) and its roads (fijāj). [[Al-aʿqāb are the routes beyond Makkah by which people come; al-anqāb are the openings of the mountains; al-fijāj are the wide roads.]] They would say to whoever travelled them: "Do not be deceived by this man among us who claims prophethood, for he is a madman," and sometimes they said "a sorcerer," sometimes "a poet," and sometimes "a soothsayer." They were called the muqtasimīn because they divided these roads among themselves. God caused them to die the worst of deaths. They had also appointed al-Walid ibn al-Mughira as arbiter at the gate of the mosque; when they asked him about the Prophet ﷺ, he would say: "Those people have spoken the truth."

The second: Qatadah said they were a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh who divided the Book of God, making part of it poetry, part of it sorcery, part of it soothsaying, and part of it "fables of the ancients."

The third: Ibn ʿAbbas said they were the People of the Book, who believed in part of it and disbelieved in part of it. Likewise ʿIkrimah said: they are the People of the Book, and they were called muqtasimīn because they were mockers, so one of them would say: "This sura is mine, and this sura is yours." This is the fourth opinion.

The fifth: Qatadah said they divided their scripture, separating it, scattering it, and distorting it.

The sixth: Zayd ibn Aslam said the intended people are the people of Salih, who swore among themselves to kill him, and so they were called muqtasimīn, as He, exalted, said: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by God that we will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾.

The seventh: al-Akhfash said they are a people who divided among themselves oaths by which they bound themselves in alliance.

It was also said that they are al-ʿĀs ibn Wa'il, ʿUtbah and Shaybah the sons of Rabiʿah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

This is the description of those who divided (the Quran). It was also said: it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "la-nas'alannahum" (surely We shall question them).

The singular of ʿiḍīn is ʿiḍah, from ʿaḍḍaytu al-shay' ta'ḍiyatan, meaning I divided it, and every division (firqah) is an ʿiḍah. Some of them said: it was originally ʿiḍwah, and the waw was dropped, which is why it was pluralised as ʿiḍīn, just as they said ʿizīn as the plural of ʿizah, whose original form is ʿizwah. Likewise thibah and thibīn. The meaning returns to what we mentioned regarding al-muqtasimīn.

"And the religion of God is not to be divided (bi-al-mu'aḍḍa)"

That is, by being divided into parts. It is also said that its root has the hāʾ dropped, and its original form is ʿiḍhah, because al-ʿiḍhah and al-ʿiḍīn in the dialect of Quraysh mean sorcery. They call a male sorcerer ʿāḍih and a female sorcerer ʿāḍihah. The poet said:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 15, verse 92–93:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do﴾. That is, We will surely question these people whose mention has preceded about what they did in the world. In al-Bukhari, it is said: Several scholars (ahl al-'ilm) said regarding His words, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do﴾, that it refers to "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah).

I say: This has also been narrated as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) hadith. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated, saying: al-Jarud ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: al-Fadl ibn Musa narrated to us, from Sharik, from Layth, from Bashir ibn Nahik, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding His words, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do﴾, he said: "About the statement 'There is no god but Allah.'" Abu 'Abd Allah said: Its meaning, in our view, is about the sincerity of "There is no god but Allah" and fulfilling it. This is because Allah, the Exalted, mentioned action in His revelation, saying, ﴿about what they used to do﴾, and did not say "about what they used to say." Although it may be permissible that speech is also an action of the tongue, what is intended is what the people of the language know: that speech is speech and action is action. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "About 'There is no god but Allah,'" meaning about fulfilling it and being truthful to its utterance. Just as al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Faith is not by adornment, nor is religion by wishful thinking, but it is what settles in the hearts and is confirmed by actions." For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah' sincerely enters Paradise." It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what is its sincerity?" He said: "That it restrains him from the prohibitions of Allah." Narrated by Zayd ibn Arqam. And from him also, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has covenanted with me that no one from my community will come to me with 'There is no god but Allah,' mixing nothing with it, except that Paradise is due to him." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is mixed with 'There is no god but Allah'?" He said: "Greed for this world, gathering it, and withholding it. They say the words of the prophets and do the deeds of tyrants." And Anas ibn Malik narrated, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'There is no god but Allah' protects the servants from the wrath of Allah as long as they do not prefer the bargain of their worldly life over their religion. When they prefer the bargain of their worldly life over their religion and then say 'There is no god but Allah,' it is returned to them, and Allah says, 'You have lied.'" Its chains are in Nawadir al-Usul.

I say: The verse, in its generality, indicates the questioning of all of them and their reckoning, the disbelievers and the believers, except those who enter Paradise without reckoning, as we have explained in the book (al-Tadhkira). If it is said: Is the disbeliever questioned and reckoned? We say: There is a difference of opinion on this, which we have mentioned in al-Tadhkira. What appears is that they are questioned, due to the verse and His words: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 72], and His words: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return; then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 38].
